entry.title: Tight limits on online selection with downward-closed constraints
entry.summary: Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies online selection problems under arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, considering different arrival orders and distributional assumptions. It establishes bounds for the standard adversarial-order prophet problem, the Bayesian random-order prophet secretary problem (and by extension the standard secretary problem), and the free-order prophet problem. Combined with earlier complementary results, these bounds pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for these variants. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give tight competitive-ratio bounds for downward-closed prophet and secretary problems across several arrival orders, reporting a superconstant separation between random-order and free-ord

entry.title: Universal optimality on finite Lee tori: which equal-size point sets minimize pair energy on finite Lee tori for all potentials of a given class.
entry.summary: Universal optimality on finite Lee tori arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies subsets of finite Lee tori that minimize pair energy among sets of the same size, for every discretely completely monotone potential. At half occupancy on a product of even cycles, the two checkerboard sets minimize both total and maximum individual energy, and they are the only minimizers for nonconstant classical completely monotone potentials, proving the checkerboard conjecture for this class. The paper also characterizes when universally optimal sets exist at the independence number and gives a characterization at density 1/5 in Z_5^n via weighted counts of pairs at distances one and two. entry.title: How expert disagreement affects LLM decision revisions
entry.summary: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper introduces a controlled two-pass audit in which a language model's question, evidence, and initial answer stay fixed while only the revision context changes: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model met the selectivity bar needed for revision to improve accuracy under expert disagreement, and accuracy fell by up to 16.1 points. The expert label increased reversals for four of the five models, but its accuracy effect ranged from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a paired two-pass audit with an exact selectivity threshold, reporting that expert labels raise reversals even with identical arguments across 1,989 decisions.

entry.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Method for Generative Visual Perception
entry.summary: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible method for turning pretrained image generators into unified multi-task visual perception systems. It analyzes design choices such as color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing, and trains 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models on public datasets. The authors also introduce legend ensembling, a test-time method that fuses segmentation results under several class-color legends and improves mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. ★★★★ Notable: The authors convert pretrained image generators into unified perception models and add legend ensembling, reporting mIoU gains on Cityscapes and COCO-Object.

entry.title: Measuring the noise floor when comparing quantized and BF16 language models
entry.summary: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper measures how much decisions change from non-quantization sources, including engine swaps, server restarts, batch-size changes and kernel selection, on 2,400 public decisions for two Cloudflare models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B). It reports quantization effects as excess over those sources. For both models, every 4-bit interval excludes all non-quantization sources, and two of five pre-registered predictions failed. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate non-quantization noise from quantization effects, measuring restarts, engines, batching, and kernels on two decision models.

entry.title: Sharp uniform Fisher information bounds from projective designs
entry.summary: Sharp Uniform Fisher Information Bounds from Projective Designs arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper studies fixed measurements for multiparameter pure-state metrology that stay informative without knowing the input state. It defines the Fisher floor as the smallest fraction of quantum Fisher information retained across all pure states and tangent directions. Bounds on this floor are derived from projective design order alone, and they approach one half, the single-copy quantum limit, as the order increases. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive dimension-independent Fisher floor guarantees from projective design order, reporting tightness at order two and odd orders, with applications to pure-state estimation.

entry.title: Near-optimal multiparameter quantum metrology using a fixed small number of measurement bases
entry.summary: Near-Optimal Multiparameter Pure-State Metrology with a Constant Number of Bases arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies multiparameter pure-state quantum metrology, where measurements optimized for different parameters are incompatible. It introduces the Fisher floor, the smallest fraction of quantum Fisher information retained across all pure states and parameter directions, as a measure of uniform sensitivity. The authors prove that a constant number of fixed orthonormal bases, independent of the Hilbert-space dimension, achieves a nearly optimal Fisher floor. They also show that d+1 mutually unbiased bases, when they exist, have a Fisher floor of at most 1/(d+1), so optimal average balance does not ensure uniform sensitivity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show a constant number of fixed orthonormal bases yields a dimension-independent near-optimal Fisher floor, with tight bounds and a contrast to MUBs.

entry.title: Observing genuine multi-time quantum memory: a quantum memory effect that only appears when three or more times are examined together
entry.summary: Observation of Genuine Multi-Time Quantum Memory arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies memory effects in open quantum systems, noting that non-Markovian dynamics alone does not prove quantum memory, since classical-memory models can reproduce it. The authors show that some quantum memory escapes all tests comparing two times and becomes detectable only when three or more times are considered jointly. They derive an analytical three-time witness and experimentally demonstrate this hierarchy on a superconducting-qubit platform with time-independent couplings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce quantum memory detectable only via three-time witnesses, derive an analytical witness, and report experimental demonstration on superconducting qubits.

entry.title: Explicit maximally entangled states in dimensions twice a prime power
entry.summary: Explicit Absolutely Maximally Entangled states in dimensions twice a prime power arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper constructs explicit families of absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states for multipartite systems with local dimension 2q, where q is an odd prime power, using a coupling of qubits and q-level systems. It gives AME(N,2q) results for several party numbers and, together with known inputs, completes the classification for nine parties: an AME(9,d) state exists if and only if d is at least 3. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct AME states in dimension 2q via a qubit-qudit coupling and report completing the nine-party classification with several explicit parameter families.

entry.title: Lattice response theory for subsystem symmetry-protected topological phases
entry.summary: Lattice response theory for subsystem symmetry-protected topological phases arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper develops a lattice response theory framework for studying subsystem symmetry-protected topological (SSPT) phases. It builds spacetime lattice gauge fields from X-type symmetry actions on qudit systems and shows that a gauge-invariant response action yields an entangler that stacks the corresponding SSPT phase. The authors also construct a new 3+1d SSPT phase protected by two 2-foliated planar subsystem symmetries and a global 0-form symmetry. ★★★★ Notable: The authors develop a lattice response framework for subsystem SPT phases and construct a new 3+1d phase with a mixed 't Hooft anomaly.

entry.title: Low-dimensional filtering for continuous quantum error correction via a classical control hierarchy
entry.summary: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper addresses the complex model estimation that limits the practicality of continuous quantum error correction by recasting it as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy. For any stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, the authors prove that the exact filter closes at dimension 3·2^(n-k-1), a dimension set by the syndrome space. They also present a committed-recovery controller that needs only 2^(n-k) class probabilities and reports higher entanglement fidelity than the compared methods in the three-qubit bit-flip code and the five-qubit perfect code. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast continuous quantum error correction filtering as a classical control hierarchy and report an exact filter dimension of 3·2^(n-k-1), a tight bound set by the syndrome space.

entry.title: Ground-State Spin Squeezing and Collective Excitations in Z2-Symmetric Systems
entry.summary: Ground-State Spin Squeezing and Collective Excitations in ℤ₂-Symmetric Systems arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies spin squeezing in the ground state of many-body quantum systems, a resource for quantum-enhanced measurements. Using the anisotropic Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, the authors show that squeezing is set by the ratio of two transverse fluctuation costs, while the collective gap is set by their geometric mean. Analyses of XXZ chains and power-law interacting systems identify a branch where squeezing and gaps increase together and squeezing persists at higher temperatures. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive an exact link between squeezing and collective excitations, identifying a gap-opening branch, checked via exact diagonalization and spin-wave analysis on XXZ chains.

entry.title: Hilbert's 17th problem for symmetric functions: undecidability and a counterexample
entry.summary: Hilbert's 17th problem for symmetric functions: undecidability and a counterexample arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies inequalities between symmetric functions that hold for every number of variables. It proves that deciding whether a rational-coefficient symmetric function is nonnegative in all dimensions is undecidable, answering a question by Acevedo, Blekherman, Debus and Riener. It also presents a degree-8 homogeneous symmetric function that is positive definite in every dimension but has no sum-of-squares multiplier uniform in the number of variables. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove dimension-free nonnegativity of symmetric functions is undecidable and give a degree-8 counterexample to uniform sum-of-squares multipliers.

entry.title: Automatic O(a) improvement for Wilson twisted mass fermions in Hamiltonian formalism
entry.summary: Automatic O(a) Improvement for Wilson Twisted Mass Fermions in the Hamiltonian Formulation arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper applies a recently developed Symanzik effective Hamiltonian framework to Wilson twisted mass fermions. The effective Hamiltonian is built only from the symmetries of the lattice Hamiltonian, without using the Euclidean spacetime Symanzik effective action. The authors use it to prove automatic O(a) improvement at maximal twist and O(a) improvement via the mass and Wilson average. They also derive the structure of the O(a) counterterms needed for clover on-shell improvement of Wilson fermions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a Hamiltonian Symanzik framework to Wilson twisted mass fermions, proving automatic O(a) improvement at maximal twist and finding the clover term splits into two independent coeffici

entry.title: Whether the channel RLD Fisher information bound can be reached asymptotically
entry.summary: Asymptotic Attainability of the Channel RLD Fisher-Information Bound arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies the channel right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information, a computable upper bound on the optimal asymptotic SLD Fisher information per channel use. It gives an exact equality criterion, a semidefinite feasibility condition involving only the Choi matrix and its first derivative. For generalized dephasing channels, the condition reduces to linear equations for nonnegative certificate weights. At a completely dephasing point, the authors compute optimal SLD information for every finite number of uses and show a repeated ancilla-free probe attains it, while the ratio of the two quantities can be unbounded. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give an exact semidefinite criterion for when the channel RLD Fisher bound is attained and compute optimal finite-use SLD information at a dephasing point.

entry.title: Learning graph states from local Pauli measurements, with tight limits for non-adaptive strategies
entry.summary: Learning Sparse Graph States with Local Pauli Measurements: Tight Nonadaptive Bounds and an Adaptive Separation arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies how many copies of an unknown n-qubit graph state are needed to identify its graph when each qubit is measured in the X, Y or Z basis. For nonadaptive strategies with d^3 ln n ≤ n, it shows that Ω(d^2 log n) copies are required, even with an unrestricted classical decoder and a small fraction of misreported edges. It also shows that adaptivity between copies can beat this barrier: on certain connected bipartite regular graphs with hidden bipartition, a breadth-first adaptive learner needs only O(d log^2 n / log log n) copies. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a tight nonadaptive lower bound of Ω(d²log n) and an adaptive separation, answering an open question on graph-state learning.

entry.title: Unified quantum-network infrastructure using optical frequency combs
entry.summary: An optical-frequency-comb-enabled unified infrastructure for quantum networks arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents an infrastructure based on optical frequency combs that carries precision timing, classical communication and quantum communication over one shared fibre link. Classical data is encoded on the comb's intensity while its pulse timing is preserved, achieving 100 Mbit/s transmission and 0.85 fs timing stability at 1 s over 100 km. The authors also analyse the excess noise introduced into a co-propagating continuous-variable quantum key distribution channel, reporting 0.0037 shot noise units of added noise and a 6.7% secret-key-rate penalty after optimization. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors unify timing, classical data and CV-QKD on one comb-based fibre link, modeling added noise; the abstract reports 100 Mbit/s and 0.85 fs stability over 100 km.

entry.title: Information thermodynamics for closed quantum many-body systems
entry.summary: Information Thermodynamics in Closed Quantum Many-Body Dynamics arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper builds an information-thermodynamic framework for closed quantum many-body systems that start in microscopic thermal equilibrium, using local measurements and finite-time controls. It proves that in the thermodynamic limit the extractable work matches that of the corresponding canonical ensemble, and expresses it via quantum-classical mutual information and Holevo information. The authors also show that feedback based on distant measurement outcomes can exploit hidden long-range correlations, extensively increasing extracted work relative to the canonical ensemble. ★★★★ Notable: The authors develop a framework for many-body quantum information thermodynamics, showing local feedback matches canonical extractable work and distant feedback exploits hidden long-range correlations

entry.title: Infinite or indefinite: query cost of simulating the quantum switch
entry.summary: Infinite or indefinite: the query cost of simulating the quantum switch arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how many calls to black-box operations a standard quantum circuit needs to reproduce the quantum switch, a device that applies two operations in a superposition of causal orders. For general channels on a d-dimensional system, the authors prove that no finite number of calls suffices for exact simulation in the worst case. They also show that approximation below error 1/2 requires a number of calls that grows with d. The paper further compares the switch with ordinary circuits in distinguishing two noise models with equal entanglement and gate fidelity. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that circuits cannot exactly simulate the quantum switch with finitely many calls, give a d^{1/4} lower bound, and show a query advantage in noise discrimination.

entry.title: Crystal-symmetry anomalies in lattice systems and a crystalline equivalence principle
entry.summary: Crystalline Equivalence Principle for Anomalies arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper gives a microscopic description of crystalline symmetry anomalies in bosonic lattice systems in one and two spatial dimensions. The authors construct anomaly indices for symmetry operators and derive their cocycle conditions and coboundary ambiguities. The results establish a crystalline equivalence principle for bosonic anomalies, and show that a nontrivial total anomaly index prevents a symmetric invertible phase. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build microscopic anomaly indices for crystalline symmetries on bosonic lattices, establish a crystalline equivalence principle, and prove obstructions to symmetric invertible phases.

entry.title: Detecting single-molecule rotational collisions using quantum logic
entry.summary: Quantum-logic detection of rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecules arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper presents a method for detecting individual rotationally inelastic collisions between single trapped molecular ions and neutral helium atoms. The researchers prepare N2+ ions in their rotational ground state, expose them to a helium beam, and identify collision events from changes in the ions' motion. Quantum-logic spectroscopy reveals the molecular state changes after collisions, and the results are compared with quantum and classical scattering calculations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors detect single rotationally inelastic collisions of trapped N2+ ions with helium using quantum-logic readout, compared against quantum and classical scattering calculations.

entry.title: Restoring Heisenberg scaling in Hamiltonian estimation under noise uncertainty
entry.summary: Restoring Heisenberg Scaling in Hamiltonian Estimation despite Noise Uncertainty arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies how uncertainty about noise parameters affects the precision of estimating Hamiltonian parameters in quantum sensors. For general Markovian dynamics under arbitrary quantum control, it derives a necessary and sufficient condition for each Hamiltonian parameter to keep Heisenberg scaling and gives its optimal asymptotic precision when the condition holds. When the condition fails, the authors propose a protocol using a noisy reference system to restore this scaling. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling under unknown Markovian noise and propose a noisy reference protocol restoring optimal precision.

entry.title: Entanglement spreading after quenches from highly entangled states
entry.summary: Going beyond the standard quasiparticle picture: Entanglement spreading after quenching from highly entangled states arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies how entanglement entropy spreads after quantum quenches in the XXZ spin chain, starting from n-rainbow states built from increasingly long-range Bell pairs. In the interacting XXZ chain, tDMRG simulations show that entropy grows at the rate thermodynamic entropy is exchanged across the cut. In the noninteracting XX chain, the quench creates entangled multiplets of 2n quasiparticle species, and a generalized quasiparticle picture captures the suppression of entanglement growth. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the quasiparticle picture to n-rainbow initial states, combining analytic results for XX chains with tDMRG simulations of the interacting XXZ chain.

entry.title: Device-independent tests for genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality in GHZ states and Bell-pair trees
entry.summary: Device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality for GHZ states and Bell-pair tree arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper derives and compares device-independent witnesses for genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) and genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) in GHZ states and trees of Bell pairs. It presents a binary-outcome family using four global measurement contexts whose tight biseparable bound does not depend on the number of parties, and a 2N-context GMNL witness for GHZ states compared with MABK and Svetlichny tests. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL respectively. The authors also benchmark these witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations with up to 10 parties. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a four-context binary-outcome GME witness with a tight party-independent biseparable bound and benchmark it on IBM Quantum GHZ states.

entry.title: Trading memory for depth: tight bounds for LCU block-encodings
entry.summary: Trading Memory for Depth: Tight Bounds for LCU Block-Encodings arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies the select depth of linear combination of unitaries (LCU) block-encodings. Grouping the terms into g parallel registers yields a depth bound set by the binning makespan and the largest bin, and the authors show a two-way reduction to classical multiprocessor scheduling so that an optimal binning attains the bound. The paper also compares two selector realisations that trade space against depth. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce LCU block-encoding select depth to multiprocessor scheduling in both directions, giving tight bounds and a memory-depth tradeoff.

entry.title: Detecting frequencies with one qubit at the discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit
entry.summary: Sensing frequencies at the discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit using a single qubit arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper studies a quantum sensing task: detecting weak oscillating fields whose strength and frequency are unknown. Prior work set a lower bound on the required sensing time, the Grover-Heisenberg limit, using a protocol that needs auxiliary qubits. The authors show that a single sensing qubit suffices for a discrete version where the signal strength is known and the frequency is drawn from a known finite set of candidates. Its sensing time grows only with the square root of the number of candidates, and this dependence is proven optimal in the worst case. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show a single qubit achieves square-root scaling in candidate frequencies and prove worst-case optimality for the discrete problem.

entry.title: Local enhancement for reliable quantum code preparation at finite measurement strength
entry.summary: Local enhancement of finite-strength code preparation: recoverability and Wilson coherence arXiv · Nov 11, 2026The paper studies preparing quantum error-correcting codes with finite-strength stabilizer measurements, which deform the encoding away from the ideal projective limit. It shows that at fixed strength, local logical leakage prevents asymptotically faithful recovery, and that enhancing only a vanishing fraction of checks near logical supports restores recoverability while the bulk stays at finite strength. The authors further find that in the three-dimensional deconfined phase, enhanced tubes restore equivalence of macroscopically separated logical representatives, whereas in two dimensions recoverability alone does not. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show local enhancement of finite-strength measurements restores recoverability, and report a dimensional distinction in logical operations between three and two dimensions. entry.title: Sketching language models for context attribution: estimating how removing prompt parts changes outputs
entry.summary: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies leave-one-out (LOO) attribution, which measures how removing each token from a prompt changes a language model's output. Under a stability assumption, it presents a sketching algorithm that estimates all LOO values to error proportional to ε with constant probability using O(√log(1/ε)/ε) evaluation calls. The authors also prove a matching lower bound in an oracle model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply forward differentiation to backpropagation circuits, reducing evaluation calls and report a matching lower bound plus a small retrieval experiment.

entry.title: Proves that checking membership in the tournament equilibrium set is PSPACE-complete
entry.summary: The Tournament Equilibrium Set Is PSPACE-Complete, Even under Hereditary Uniqueness arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies the tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), a voting rule proposed by Schwartz in 1990 that relies on pairwise majority comparisons and is defined recursively. It proves that deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ is PSPACE-complete, closing the gap between the previously known NP-hardness and PSPACE membership. The hardness holds even when every nonempty subtournament has a unique minimal retentive set. The paper also shows how the complexity changes with the bound on the number of dominators. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove TEQ membership is PSPACE-complete, even under hereditary uniqueness, and give a fuller dominator-bound complexity classification for tournament solutions.

entry.title: A theory of learnability through debate
entry.summary: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies debate as a training method, in which two models argue for opposite answers and a human judge decides. The authors formalize the learning process as an online learning problem and show that the best way to learn with a judge can differ from adversarial debate. They define a cooperative version of the protocol and characterize its learnability using a combinatorial dimension. They also show that a small number of incorrect judgments can cause a large learning error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formulate debate training as online learning, propose a cooperative variant characterized by a combinatorial dimension, and show few judging errors can cause large learning error.

entry.title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Texture Descriptors with Exact Binary Inference
entry.summary: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper presents FLEX-LBP, a method that learns the radius, sampling angles, color transform, and thresholds of Local Binary Patterns (LBP), a widely used texture descriptor, via backpropagation. Forward passes compute exact binary codes and hard histogram counts, so the deployed descriptor remains an interpretable hard-binary LBP with 90 learnable parameters and unchanged inference cost. The authors compare configurations on six color texture benchmarks against five classical LBP-family descriptors, PCANet, a neural LBP, and frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features. ★★★★ Notable: The authors learn LBP radii, angles, color transform and thresholds via backpropagation while keeping exact binary forward passes; the report covers six color texture benchmarks over five seeds.

entry.title: Submodular secretary problem: tight 1-1/e for monotone objectives, and a ratio strictly between 1/e and 1/2 in general
entry.summary: The Submodular Secretary Problem: Tight 1-1/e for Monotone Objectives, and Strictly Between 1/e and 1/2 in General arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper studies the submodular secretary problem with a cardinality constraint, where elements arrive in random order and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably to maximize a nonnegative submodular function over sets of at most k elements. For monotone objectives, the optimal competitive ratio tends to exactly 1-1/e as k grows, achieved by an algorithm using at most 4n+1 value queries. For general objectives, the optimal limiting ratio is shown to lie strictly between 1/e and 1/2, using a new technique called eligibility attenuation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a tight 1-1/e ratio for monotone objectives with one algorithm, and improve general objectives to a value strictly between 1/e and 1/2 via eligibility attenuation.

entry.title: "Sowing the Seeds of Intractability: Kalah is PSPACE-complete" — a proof that deciding a forced win in the sowing game Kalah is PSPACE-complete as board size grows
entry.summary: Sowing the Seeds of Intractability: Kalah is PSPACE-complete arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies Kalah, a classic two-player sowing game in the mancala family, with the number of pits per side treated as part of the input. It shows that deciding whether a designated player can force a win from an arbitrary position is PSPACE-complete. The proof introduces an intermediate game, Line Kalah, reduces quantified Boolean formulas to it, and embeds the line positions into Kalah with both stores empty. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that deciding forced wins in generalized Kalah is PSPACE-complete via a reduction from QBF through an intermediate Line Kalah problem, valid under both capture conventions and bonus

entry.title: Polynomial-time linear regression under self-selection bias
entry.summary: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies estimating k linear regressors under self-selection bias, up to error ε, using the maximum self-selection criterion. The authors give an algorithm running in polynomial time in n, k, and 1/ε for the unknown-index variant, which also handles correlated noise between regressors, a setting related to max-affine regression. Their method analyzes high-degree Hermite moments of the covariates, which approximately decompose into sums of tensor powers of the regressors, followed by tensor decomposition and a least-squares step. ★★★★ Notable: The authors replace exhaustive search with a tensor decomposition of high-order Hermite covariate moments, giving a polynomial-time algorithm for self-selection regression that also covers correlated

entry.title: Combinatorial Bernoulli factories with polynomially many coins
entry.summary: Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper presents an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories, which convert coins with unknown biases into a random vertex of a polytope whose mean is exactly the unknown value. For every affine slice of the cube, it gives a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time are polynomial in the dimension and in 1/δ*. For perfect matchings this yields O(n^8 δ*^-2 log(n/δ*)) flips, whereas the prior factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider (STOC 2021) needs at least n^(2n-1) expected flips at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a single algorithm for every affine cube slice, with expected coin flips polynomial in dimension and 1/δ*, and report polynomial bounds for perfect matchings versus prior exponential

entry.title: Adding Deliberate Feedback Delays to Adversarial MDPs for Optimal Regret Bounds
entry.summary: Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal √ S and √ K Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies regret minimization in episodic adversarial Markov decision processes with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. The authors propose a technique called introduced feedback delays, which estimates the current policy's Q-function using future episodes while still updating the policy. It uses Geometric Resampling with Rejection and thresholded visitation probabilities to handle policy changes during the delay. The paper reports high-probability regret of $\tilde O(\text{poly}(H)\sqrt{SAK})$ in tabular AMDPs, resolving an open problem, and $\tilde O(\text{poly}(d,H)\sqrt K)$ in linear AMDPs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce voluntary feedback delays with geometric resampling, reporting optimal √S regret in tabular and √K regret in linear AMDPs.

entry.title: Consensus capture in drone video stabilization on busy urban scenes
entry.summary: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper studies reference-frame stabilization of hovering drone video in scenes with moving vehicles, where the robust homography estimate can be pulled toward a group's motion. The authors build a two-part benchmark with static and dynamic protocols that score ten registration pipelines against pseudo-ground-truth references. They report that masking moving objects removes this consensus capture for every pipeline while leaving the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce consensus capture and a static and dynamic benchmark, scoring ten UAV stabilization pipelines, with masking shown to remove capture.

entry.title: Symmetry in Time: Representation theory of how linear recurrent models remember sequences
entry.summary: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper uses representation theory to analyze state space models (SSMs), showing that diagonal recurrent updates can only track commutative groups. The authors introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training, and report that it solves group tasks exactly, including S5 with 32 generators. They also show that the learned weights can be interpreted to recover a gyroscope's calibration, imperfect qubit gate rotations, and protein backbone geometry. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use representation theory to characterize state tracking in linear recurrent memory and propose HyperSSM with quaternion channels, reporting exact group-task solutions including S5 and 25x

entry.title: Cited but Unused: Provenance Problems in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
entry.summary: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper finds that citations attached by retrieval-augmented generation systems often misstate where an answer actually came from. By substituting false values for facts in retrieved passages and re-querying, the authors measure that 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims across several model sizes derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. They also report that natural language inference verification performs at chance level and that models tend to select citations that agree with their own outputs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose counterfactual value substitution to measure citation provenance, reporting 1.2% to 15.7% of claims from parametric memory and comparing ten attribution methods.

entry.title: Learning dynamics of a spatial game on resource landscapes
entry.summary: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper introduces the influencer's game, a spatial game in which players occupy positions in a trait space and receive shares of resources based on their relative influence at each trait point. The authors show that a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium exists when the influence kernel is strictly log-concave, and they analyze how stability depends on kernel parameters, player count, and resource distribution shape. Beyond the equilibrium analysis, the paper identifies stability thresholds and bifurcation types, and it supports the results with real-world resource data and multi-agent reinforcement learning experiments. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new spatial game, prove a unique symmetric equilibrium, derive a stability threshold and bifurcations, and test with real data and reinforcement learning.

entry.title: HiVE-VQA: Video quality assessment using hierarchical features from a frozen video encoder
entry.summary: HiVE-VQA: Hierarchical Interaction via Volumetric Embedding for Video Quality Assessment arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper presents HiVE-VQA, presented as the first framework to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to no-reference video quality assessment. It extracts features from multiple depths of a frozen pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, stacks them into a spatio-temporal volume, and fuses them with a compact 3D convolutional head of about 5.2M trainable parameters. Trained only on LSVQ without fine-tuning, it reports higher SROCC and PLCC than 17 state-of-the-art methods on intra- and cross-dataset benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a frozen JEPA video encoder with hierarchical 3D convolutional fusion to no-reference VQA, reporting gains over 17 SOTA methods across four benchmarks.

entry.title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
entry.summary: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper presents ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a transformer model for steady, boundary-driven partial differential equations. No learned operation takes raw coordinates as input, and sums over the boundary are computed as quadratures, so the model stays consistent under rigid motions, reflections, unit changes, and mesh refinement. On AeroZoo, a set of 2,816 flows varying in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline. On AirfRANS, its errors are second only to the boundary-integral model GLOBE and at least 1.6 times lower than Transolver and GeoTransolver. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build rigid-motion and unit invariance into slice attention and report lower errors than baselines on AeroZoo and AirfRANS.

entry.title: Keeping the Flaw, Silencing the Alert: Testing CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
entry.summary: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper tests how robust CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking is to natural rewrites that keep a vulnerability intact. A large language model, without knowing the analyzer's internals, rewrote one function on each reported flow, and the flaw survived while the alert disappeared for 26.2% of 172 real npm flows. All silencing rewrites trace to seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and many also fool other taint analyzers. The authors conclude that a vanished alert is weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors test CodeQL taint tracking with vulnerability-preserving rewrites on 172 real npm flows, silencing 26.2%, traced to seven library-modeling gaps and cross-checked on other analyzers.

entry.title: A unified framework for Bellman contraction under MMD
entry.summary: Bellman Contraction under MMD: A Unified Framework arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper presents a mathematical framework for studying contraction of the distributional Bellman operator under Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). It shows that contraction reduces to conditional positive definiteness of a kernel built from the base kernel, and uses Schoenberg's theorem and Bernstein functions to derive criteria for radial kernels. The framework unifies known results for several kernels and numerical search identifies 11 new kernels that induce contraction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce MMD contraction of the distributional Bellman operator to conditional positive definiteness and report 11 new contracting kernels via Schoenberg's theorem.

entry.title: Oracle-efficient algorithm with near-optimal regret for adversarial contextual bandits
entry.summary: Near-Optimal Regret for Oracle-Efficient Adversarial Contextual Bandits arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies contextual bandits with K actions, N policies, and i.i.d. contexts the learner can sample. The authors give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret O(√(KT log(2N)) log(2KT)) against the best policy in hindsight, improving the T^{2/3} horizon dependence of prior oracle-efficient bounds and matching the optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. The method perturbs policy scores using Laplace noise at Poisson-sampled auxiliary contexts, with scales approximated by projected stochastic gradient descent using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimization oracle. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve oracle-efficient adversarial contextual bandit regret from T^{2/3} to near-optimal √T order, using Laplace perturbations and projected SGD.

entry.title: Optimal Tokenization Disambiguation for Secure Linguistic Steganography
entry.summary: Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography arXiv · Nov 13, 2026The paper addresses a flaw in provably secure linguistic steganography, where ambiguous tokenizations prevent the receiver from extracting the hidden message reliably. The authors prove that a single-history receiver must give up stop entropy, and they propose coin projection, a closed-form scheme that reaches this bound. Experiments on English, Chinese and Japanese show that coin projection retains 91-93% of string entropy and converts 2.16 to 6.85 times more entropy into message bits than SyncPool. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a single-history receiver must give up stop entropy, and present a closed-form coin projection scheme attaining this bound, compared against SyncPool on English, Chinese, and Japanes

entry.title: Evolving programs to discover effective memory designs for AI agents
entry.summary: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper introduces MAPE, a framework that evolves complete memory programs for agents starting from minimal seeds, using a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, it reports accuracy gains of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost. The authors identify two recurring design patterns: keeping raw conversations as retrievable evidence and composing retrieved evidence according to query intent. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evolve agent memory programs and report up to 12% accuracy gain on LoCoMo and LongMemEval at 35% serving cost, plus transferable composition module.

entry.title: Auditing AI reviewers with a benchmark on real papers
entry.summary: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper introduces a benchmark that injects objective errors of four types (general, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real arXiv papers, measuring each AI reviewer's detection rate and false-positive rate on clean copies. It also presents Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies claims by retrieving cited papers, using computer algebra, and running numerical code. Evaluating twelve reviewer systems on astrophysics and machine learning corpora with 357 injected errors, the authors find that model choice has the largest effect on detection rate, while tools help mainly where the model cannot supply the capability itself. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a benchmark injecting 357 localisable errors into real astrophysics and ML preprints, and a multi-agent reviewer using retrieval, computer algebra, and executed code across twelv

entry.title: Your vision model may be secretly good at reading brain signals (EEG)
entry.summary: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper shows that a vision foundation model never trained on EEG can outperform specialized EEG foundation models when EEG signals are rendered as images. The proposed SeeEEG method keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed, using at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. On eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, SeeEEG with a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B beats seven EEG foundation models in balanced accuracy on all eight. The learned displays also transfer to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors render EEG as images for a frozen vision transformer, learning only display parameters, and report beating seven EEG foundation models on eight datasets with a random-init control.

entry.title: DPA: A decentralized learning method for highly varied local data
entry.summary: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper proposes Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), an algorithm for training deep learning models across networked agents while keeping data local. DPA combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer to address performance loss caused by heterogeneous local data. The authors give a convergence bound for smooth nonconvex objectives and introduce DPA-1G, which uses one communication round per iteration. In experiments on the GUT benchmark, DPA outperforms several baselines, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. ★★★★ Notable: Extends centralized primal averaging to decentralized training with quasi-global momentum, avoiding tracking variables; the authors report gains over several baselines on GUT benchmarks, largest on sp

entry.title: Explicit codes correcting insertions, deletions, and substitutions via multicoloring
entry.summary: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper constructs explicit q-ary codes of length n that correct any combination of at most t insertions, deletions, and substitutions. Their redundancy is 2t·log_q n plus O(log log n) q-ary symbols, matching the leading term of Levenshtein's classical existential bound. The approach uses a prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph, and the construction supports deterministic encoding and decoding. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use prime-based multicoloring of the edit-confusion graph to match Levenshtein's leading redundancy term 2t log_q n, with deterministic encoding and decoding time bounds.

entry.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field: a model where the floor itself computes
entry.summary: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper introduces CABOT, a model in which the discrete plane robots move on is an active cellular automaton rather than a passive stage. The robots are deliberately weak, seeing only nearby cell states and robot positions, so the number of floor states becomes the measure of required resources. The authors show that a handful of states enables line formation, gathering and exploration, and prove that gathering and line formation cannot be solved when the floor must stay silent. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast the grid floor as a cellular automaton, reporting solvability and impossibility results for line formation, gathering and exploration with few states.

entry.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs
entry.summary: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper argues that cross-modal alignment alone loses information when modalities are informationally asymmetric, as in visual question answering. It proposes Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA), which splits latent representations into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers that capture what alignment discards. On compositional reasoning benchmarks, D-JEPA substantially outperforms alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove an alignment redundancy bound and propose D-JEPA, splitting latents into shared and private fibers, evaluated on compositional reasoning benchmarks.

entry.title: Treating Safety as a Budget: Calibrating the Control Channel of Constrained GRPO for Vision-Language Models
entry.summary: Safety as a Budget: Calibrating the Control Channel of Constrained GRPO for Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how reinforcement learning can train vision-language models to refuse harmful image-text requests while keeping safety expressed as budgets on harmful assistance and over-refusal. Enforced with Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO, the approach fails because the scorer's mean bias decides whether the multiplier converges, saturates or switches off, and standard group-wise standardization cancels the multiplier. The authors propose two-channel constrained GRPO, which keeps raw scores for the base reward, calibrates penalties through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled responses, and preserves the multiplier in the advantage. On Qwen3-VL-2B, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, with over-refusal at most 2%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify two failure modes in constrained GRPO for VLM safety, scorer mean bias and within-group standardization cancelling the multiplier, and propose a two-channel fix. entry.title: Singularity-Bench: Can AI Agents Build Other AI Agents? A Benchmark for Autonomous AI Development
entry.summary: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents? arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper introduces Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark testing whether AI agents can autonomously develop AI systems across six end-to-end tasks, including pre-training, post-training, inference, and cluster orchestration. Agents implement core systems from a minimal starting point and are compared against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. The authors also found reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the Harbor framework and developed Breakwater, an extension that blocks the attacks they tested. Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matched or outperformed the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, while the other agents averaged 0.58. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evaluate agents on six end-to-end AI-development tasks against human baselines and report reward-hacking flaws in Harbor, plus a patched extension.

entry.title: Linear-order improvement of the Gilbert-Varshamov bound for linear and quantum codes
entry.summary: A Theta(n)-Multiplicative Improvement of the Gilbert-Varshamov Bound for Linear and Quantum Codes arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper concerns the Gilbert-Varshamov bound, a standard benchmark for the existence of error-correcting codes. For q-ary linear codes, the best previously known general improvement was of order Θ(√n). The authors use a new viewpoint that tolerates O(n) low-weight points and removes them together at the cost of one dimension, yielding a Θ(n) multiplicative improvement for linear codes of arbitrary rate. The method is also extended to quantum codes, giving a Θ(n) improvement of the quantum GV bound for a stated range of relative distances. ★★★★ Notable: The authors achieve a Θ(n)-multiplicative GV improvement for linear codes by allowing O(n) low-weight points and eliminating them jointly, extended to quantum codes.

entry.title: Exact quantum algorithms for composed Boolean functions
entry.summary: Exact Quantum Algorithms for Composed Boolean Functions arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies exact quantum algorithms for block compositions of total Boolean functions and proves an upper bound on exact quantum query complexity in terms of the outer function's exact query complexity and polynomial degree. Applied to recursive ternary not-all-equal and other fixed gadgets, it yields improved exact rates. The composition technique also transfers separations from approximate query complexity and degree to exact quantum query complexity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a composition construction whose costs are governed by exact query complexity and degree, improving separation exponents.

entry.title: Bait: A defense against harmful agentic reinforcement learning by probing the reward function
entry.summary: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper shows that safety alignment of a large language model can be fully undone through harmful agentic reinforcement learning run via a service API, at a cost of about $20. The authors propose Bait, a defense that proactively probes the reward function to block learning from harmful rewards. Experiments indicate Bait still allows learning from benign reward functions, and analysis suggests an adaptive attacker aware of Bait cannot perfectly subvert it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors expose a safety vulnerability in agentic RL services and propose Bait, a defense probing the reward function; experiments report mitigation of harmful learning.

entry.title: Cost of force-closing a Lightning channel: analysis of 974,000 channel closes, 2018–2026
entry.summary: What Does It Cost to Force-Close a Lightning Channel? Evidence from 974,000 Channel Closes, 2018-2026 arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper traces 973,581 Lightning Network channel closes from January 2018 to October 2026 on-chain and cross-checks 698,476 public closes with a separate chain index. It finds that fee spikes did not produce a wave of force closes. Force closes cost two to six times as much in fees as cooperative closes. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors measure force-close costs across fee regimes using 973,581 channel closes, informing zero-fee commitment and anchor-output design decisions.

entry.title: Smoothed Analysis for Distributed Maximal Independent Set
entry.summary: Smoothed Analysis for Distributed MIS arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies smoothed analysis of the distributed Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem, where each edge of an arbitrary base graph is independently toggled with probability p. When p is about β·ln n/n for a large constant β, a randomized LOCAL algorithm computes an MIS in O(√log n) rounds with high probability, beating the worst-case lower bound. Conversely, for p at most (1/2−δ)·ln n/n, some base graph forces every randomized LOCAL algorithm to need Ω(log n/log log n) rounds, so the smoothing required is optimal up to a constant factor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply smoothed analysis to distributed MIS, reporting O(√log n)-round randomized LOCAL algorithms and a nearly tight matching lower bound.

entry.title: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework Combining PyTorch-style Modularity with Megakernel Speed
entry.summary: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper presents MegaOps, a framework that keeps the one-GPU-kernel-per-operator design of PyTorch-style ML frameworks while removing barriers between dependent kernels. Instead of fusing operators into a single megakernel, it runs dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and synchronizes them on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor. Evaluated on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models across H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and multi-GPU servers, MegaOps matches hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernel throughput. It reaches 1.09 to 1.10 times the best baseline's decode throughput and 0.98 to 1.10 times its prefill throughput. ★★★★ Notable: The authors remove kernel barriers via tile-level dependencies without fusing kernels, reporting parity with ThunderKittens megakernels and 1.09-1.10x decode throughput on Llama3 and Qwen3.

entry.title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching via Image-Editor Controls
entry.summary: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents ATune, a photo retouching model trained without expert-edited pairs, using degraded versions of millions of good photographs instead. It learns target values for 13 measurable attributes such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, then searches the sliders of an existing photo editor to reach them. Each edit is a readable list of slider values. In a user study with 157 raters, its edits were preferred over some rival outputs, and in comparisons against supervised methods raters chose ATune 46.3% of the time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors learn retouching without expert edits by degrading photos into training pairs, outputting readable editor slider values, and report comparisons on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ.

entry.title: Generating Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Models
entry.summary: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper asks whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn reviewed examples of Linux kernel driver conversions into Coccinelle semantic patches. The authors propose a guided generation framework that splits examples into change variants, generates and repairs rules using feedback, and uses a compile critic to reject rules whose output does not build. On a pre-registered test set of 122 held-out driver conversions, the framework lets a local model solve about 35 conversions on average, fewer than Spinfer (41) and a frontier LLM agent (66), but with the highest precision. All code, prompts, responses and results are released. ★★★★ Notable: The authors adapt guided generation to synthesize Coccinelle semantic patches for kernel API migrations, using a compile critic. entry.title: Concatenated codes with one inner code achieving low-rate Gilbert-Varshamov distance
entry.summary: Concatenated Codes with One Inner Code: Low-Rate Gilbert-Varshamov Asymptotics from Algebraic-Geometric Codes arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies concatenated codes that use one binary inner code for all outer coordinates, with outer codes taken as random subcodes of scaled algebraic codes. It gives a general upper bound on the probability that the minimum distance fails, along with conditions for exponential decay. Using algebraic-geometric codes from the Garcia-Stichtenoth tower, it constructs random binary codes with rates approaching ε² whose distance matches the leading coefficient of the Gilbert-Varshamov bound at low rates, with polynomial-time encoding and unique decoding. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine one inner code with subcodes of Garcia-Stichtenoth algebraic-geometry codes, reporting a low-rate GV-matching distance bound with exponential failure probability.

entry.title: PolicySniff: a side-channel attack that infers an LLM agent's approval-policy setting from shared-GPU timing
entry.summary: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper presents PolicySniff, a method by which a co-resident attacker on the same GPU infers which approval-policy setting an LLM agent is using, by timing only its own GPU kernels. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, it identified the deployed setting with 94.17% balanced accuracy. The authors conclude that behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality, so operators should measure distinguishability on their serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show GPU-sharing timing side channels can infer an LLM agent's approval policy, reporting 94.17% balanced accuracy on a sparse MoE runtime.

entry.title: Intent-aware protection for AI agents: using deployed purpose as a security reference
entry.summary: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper notes that existing defenses mainly detect prompt injection or harmful outputs and cannot tell whether an AI agent still serves its deployed purpose. The authors propose Intent-Aware Security, defining Intent Preservation and Intent Drift through an Intent Profile built from organizational, role, and developer intent. They present an 887-sample benchmark across 35 agents and four profile-based protections, which outperform profile-free baselines on their evaluations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat trusted agent intent as a security object, define intent drift, and report gains over baselines on their benchmark and AgentDojo trajectories.

entry.title: A matching lower bound for online smooth calibration
entry.summary: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, a measure of how far probabilistic forecasts are from being calibrated that is robust to small perturbations. The authors construct a new adaptive adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual, making it costly to compensate for past residuals. They show every forecaster incurs expected smooth calibration error of order √T, matching the known upper bound up to universal constants. The result also yields Ω(√T) lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a new adaptive adversary giving an Ω(√T) minimax lower bound on online smooth calibration error, matching the known upper bound.

entry.title: Optimal integer masks limiting one-guess attacks under a mask-cost budget
entry.summary: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper studies the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer mask, with the mask's absolute moment bounded. For a uniform secret on an interval, the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit, the paper characterises masks that do not increase success over the prior baseline, determines their minimal cost, and gives the full cost-vulnerability frontier for every bias. ★★★★ Notable: The authors exactly characterise the cost-vulnerability frontier of additive integer masks, showing infinitely many piecewise-linear pieces accumulating at a critical cost, for uniform and biased-bit

entry.title: Human Capital in Context: Employment Survival and Worker-Firm Match Quality
entry.summary: Human Capital in Context: What Employment Survival Reveals About Worker-Firm Match arXiv · Nov 12, 2026The paper proposes a measure of worker-firm match quality that treats fit as a property of the pair, learned from how long employment relationships survive. A two-tower neural network embeds workers and firms into a common space, with match quality given by the cosine similarity of the two vectors. Estimated on over a billion person-periods, a 0.1 increase in match quality is associated with a 48% reduction in the odds of separation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat worker-firm match quality as a pair property learned from employment survival with a two-tower network. entry.title: Study of privacy leakage from recurrent state in LLM inference
entry.summary: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how personalized LLM services compress private context into fixed-size recurrent state that can still be inferred after public dialogue. The authors probe partial states and observe GPU power during inference across released hybrid models. They find that private facts and personal attributes can be recovered and can change later decisions, and that whole-device power can reveal information such as age. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend recurrent-state privacy leakage to persistence and GPU power side channels, reporting probing experiments and an unprivileged age inference on a partitioned GPU, affecting serving a

entry.title: Reaching Majority Consensus in h-Majority Opinion Dynamics via First-Repetition Rules (Paper)
entry.summary: Plurality Consensus for h-Majority via First-Repetition Rules arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies h-Majority dynamics, in which n agents holding one of k opinions each round sample h agents and adopt the most frequent opinion among them. The authors show that for any h≥3, if the initial majority's bias is large enough, consensus on the initially most frequent opinion is reached with high probability within O((1+n/(h²M₀)) log n) rounds. The central tool is a comparison principle showing that, among symmetric rules, plurality maximizes the gap between the most frequent opinion and any competitor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a comparison principle to reduce one round of h-Majority to DejaVu, obtaining an O((1+n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) consensus time bound under a bias condition.

entry.title: Predicting Needles in Petabyte-Scale Satellite Imagery: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation
entry.summary: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper represents change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings from different time points, enabling automated global event discovery in satellite imagery without manual annotation. The authors build a dataset of over 21,000 locations, more than 64 event types, and about 2 million PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 images across six continents, and use it to train a global event anticipation model. According to the paper, the model reaches a maximum F1 score of 93.5% for change detection, outperforms baselines 3.6 times on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error up to nine months before completion. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors represent change as embedding differences, build a 2M-image global event dataset, and report 93.5% max F1 and 3.6x retrieval gains.

entry.title: PhysICL: In-context learning of physical fields on unstructured meshes using procedural priors
entry.summary: PhysICL: In-Context Learning of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes from Procedural Priors arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents PhysICL, a model pretrained solely on procedurally generated tasks that predicts physical fields directly on unstructured query meshes from labeled simulation examples, without updating its weights. On five PLAID datasets not seen during pretraining, prediction error decreases as the number of context examples grows. It performs comparably to per-dataset reduced-order models on two of the datasets. ★★★★ Notable: The authors transfer in-context learning to physical field prediction on unstructured meshes, pretrained only on procedural priors and tested on five unseen PLAID datasets.

entry.title: Sparse PCA with overlapping supports: hardness and an approximation scheme
entry.summary: Sparse PCA with Overlapping Supports: NP-Hardness and an FPTAS arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies sparse principal component analysis with several components, where each component must be sparse and all components must be pairwise orthogonal, and their supports may overlap arbitrarily. The authors show the problem is NP-hard even with two components and rank two, but admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme when the rank and number of components are fixed. The returned solution has exactly orthonormal columns. The approach reduces the problem to a sparse orthogonal Procrustes problem, combining approximate dynamic programming over rows with two-column updates. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show NP-hardness for general overlapping supports and give an FPTAS for fixed r and d, extending known disjoint and common-support results.

entry.title: Physics-based simulation for scalable, generalizable MRI reconstruction
entry.summary: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper introduces the Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), which trains on physics-simulated data and co-designs its architecture and learning methods around scalability to improve MRI reconstruction across unseen conditions. It was evaluated on 14 public and in-house datasets spanning seven centers, five vendors, field strengths from 0.3 to 7 T, and many anatomical regions and protocols. The authors report that SIM recovers fine anatomical details and suppresses aliasing artifacts on zero-shot cases where conventional deep-learning methods fail. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors co-design physics-simulated training data, architecture, and learning for zero-shot MRI reconstruction, validated across 14 datasets and a blinded radiologist study.

entry.title: Beyond Reweighting: Certified Gains from New Transitions in Discrete MCMC
entry.summary: Beyond Reweighting: Certified Improvements from New Transitions in Discrete MCMC arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how to design the set of allowed transitions in reversible Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), considering both the transitions and their stationary flows. It gives a necessary and sufficient dual condition under which adding transitions strictly lowers the optimal asymptotic variance, along with computable primal-dual certificates. On identical augmented Ising supports, full weight optimization certified strict improvements in 24 of 24 conditions, while degree-based Metropolis-Hastings weighting certified none. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a dual necessary and sufficient condition for support augmentation to strictly improve asymptotic variance, construct a family with Ω(n) gains from one edge, and report experiments on

entry.title: Mechanistic interpretability study of AION-1, an astronomy AI model
entry.summary: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper presents a causal mechanistic interpretability study of AION-1, an astronomy foundation model, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. The advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies and is mostly localized to the encoder's first block. A single attention head is necessary for most of the advantage, but none of the tested astrophysical operations explains what it computes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first causal interpretability study of astronomy model AION-1, localizing its multimodal redshift advantage to one block and a single attention head.

entry.title: Differential Backpack language models: letting context suppress word senses
entry.summary: Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights arXiv · Nov 12, 2026Backpack language models predict by linearly combining context-free per-word sense vectors with non-negative context weights. This paper computes those weights with differential attention, letting context actively inhibit a sense, which the authors call a differential Backpack. At equal parameter counts it reduces the perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% on WikiText-103 and keeps an advantage up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText. Its sense representations also improve zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors replace non-negative softmax weights with differential attention so context can inhibit senses, reporting perplexity gains on WikiText-103 and OpenWebText with ablations.

entry.title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Peak Estimation from Solution Contours
entry.summary: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions arXiv · Nov 12, 2026Evolutionary algorithms usually use their evaluated candidate solutions only to rank individuals. This paper treats these solutions as elevation points, draws contour lines through them, and splits the search region into peaks, with a peak memory directing the search toward new ones. It proposes CA-EA and CA-SAEA, which are tested on two-dimensional benchmarks and the CEC 2015 expensive suite. Their performance relative to competing methods varies across settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat evaluated solutions as contour maps to decompose peaks and extrapolate their locations, reporting results on 2-D benchmarks and CEC 2015 expensive problems.

entry.title: Data-free metrics for neural network layers may not reflect model quality
entry.summary: Data-Free Metrics Don't Work: The Missing Invariance Under Functionally Preserving Reparameterisations arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper examines data-free metrics from random matrix theory (RMT), which are used to judge the quality of neural network layers and pre-trained models. The authors show that functionally preserving reparametrisations, made by reinitialising robust layers, can give these metrics arbitrary values across several architectures and scales. They also find that relationships among RMT metrics are spuriously linked to generalisation, and that whether models land in a 'good' metric range depends partly on initialisation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show RMT-based data-free metrics can be arbitrary via functionally preserving reparameterisations, across several architectures and scales.

entry.title: Hidden Image Attacks: Recovering Secret Content from Deep Hiding Models
entry.summary: Your Secrets Are Showing: Deep Image Hiding Models Are Surprisingly Easy to Attack arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper examines whether an attacker can identify what a hidden image depicts without knowing which model concealed it. The authors built a dataset from 11 deep hiding models and trained a single decoder that extracts secret content from unseen models, recognizable by both humans and machines. The attack also works on out-of-distribution secrets, multi-image hiding, and exposes private content hidden by AIRPNet. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show a single decoder extracts hidden secrets across 11 deep hiding models, strengthened via frequency-guided training, with implications for steganographic privacy.

entry.title: The Golden Ratio: Fair Splitting of Goods with EF1 and Ordinal MMS
entry.summary: The Golden Ratio: EF1 and Ordinal-MMS for Additive Goods arXiv · Nov 12, 2026This paper studies how to fairly divide goods among agents. For additive valuations, it proves that a complete allocation always exists that is both envy-free up to one good (EF1) and satisfies 1-out-of-⌊φn⌋ ordinal maximin share (MMS), where φ is the golden ratio. For bivalued valuations, where each agent has two non-negative values per good, it obtains a complete allocation that is both EFX and satisfies 1-out-of-⌈(7n-1)/6⌉ MMS. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove EF1 plus 1-out-of-floor(phi n) MMS for additive goods, improving prior bounds, and an EFX plus MMS result for bivalued valuations.

entry.title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Framework for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
entry.summary: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper argues that long-lived personal AI agents lack an incentive layer and models incentives as runtime contracts over operating parameters such as model tier, compute, memory budget, and tool authority, rather than as prompt text. It presents a principal-agent model with hidden effort and costly verification, with several derived results. In experiments, prompt-level incentive framing had no detectable effect, while runtime allocation raised success on the hardest task family at a higher cost. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize incentives as runtime contracts over an agent's operating point, giving a principal-agent model and a non-consumption invariance principle; experiments comprise 240 real-LLM runs

entry.title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: How People Are Fooled by PDF Signatures
entry.summary: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper introduces Genuine PDF Forgeries, an attack that exploits the gap between cryptographically verified signer certificates and the signature blocks people see in PDF documents. The authors tested 23 PDF viewers and validation tools, finding that nine of the 13 that automatically report validity hide authenticated signer details behind extra user actions. Online studies with 584 EU participants and a real-world test within two organizations assessed how often the forged visual identity was accepted. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new attack class exploiting mismatches between visible signature blocks and certificates, tested on 23 viewers and 584 participants.

entry.title: Correct Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Auditing Whether Audio AI Really Tells Sounds Apart
entry.summary: Right Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Source-Level Counterfactual Auditing of Large Audio-Language Models arXiv · Nov 11, 2026The paper introduces TRACE, a method that removes the queried sound source and each rival source in turn, then checks whether every version still containing the sound scores higher than the version without it. Testing 8 large audio-language models on 3,456 controlled mixtures, it finds that 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering check. The authors argue that accuracy only certifies an answer, while TRACE audits whether a model ranks sound presence above absence. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose TRACE, a source-deletion counterfactual ordering audit, reporting results across 8 LALMs and 3,456 mixtures.

entry.title: Reading and Then Ignoring: How Self-Directed LLM Agents Behave in Public Services
entry.summary: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper tests ten large language models under four prompt conditions across four expert-validated public-service scenarios, collecting 2,400 trajectories and comparing them with 1,000 runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in most open-ended runs but produced an artifact or self-chosen task in only a small share, and adding domain context barely changed that rate. The authors propose a test that public-service institutions can run on their own records before procurement, and they release the scenarios, code, and trajectories. ★★★★ Notable: The authors test autonomous LLM agents in public-service scenarios, reporting 2,400 trajectories and 1,000 context-free sandbox runs.

entry.title: Verifier choice affects text-to-image counting benchmark results
entry.summary: Verifier Choice is a Benchmark Design Variable: Auditing Structural Counting Evaluation in Text-to-Image Models arXiv · Nov 11, 2026This paper examines whether the automatic verifiers used to score text-to-image benchmarks are reliable, focusing on counting objects in generated images. The authors build a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects and compare several multimodal verifiers and protocols against human-visible counts across 6,240 images. They find that verifier and protocol choices change measured reliability and can reverse the human ordering of generators.
