entry.summary: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper reproduces two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, for the CAGE Challenge 4 cyber-defense benchmark. It finds that the simulator silently discards actions sent to agents still busy with a previous action, and that the documented observation does not expose this busy state, affecting reported scores and training outcomes. The authors also note that evaluation fixes the environment seed but not the policy seed, and that five published comparison tables omit the details needed to compare their numbers. The authors release their tools, patches, traces, checkpoints and a disclosure checklist. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reproduce reference defenders and report that busy-agent actions are silently discarded and mis-scored, quantifying score shifts and auditing five published tables.

entry.title: HiPFuse: real-time LiDAR segmentation for robot perception on edge devices
entry.summary: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper presents HiPFuse, a framework that fuses point features with bird's-eye-view (BEV) features to label LiDAR scans in real time on resource-limited devices. It exchanges height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales and adds a dual-scale BEV context module using a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD it reports 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, above the 10 Hz scan rate. Replacing the semantic front end in a robotic odometry system reduces absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a point-BEV fusion framework with height-partitioned features, auxiliary supervision, and a dual-scale context module, reporting real-time results on SemanticKITTI and MCD.

entry.title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Testing Whether Vision-Language Models Can Follow Personal Privacy Rules
entry.summary: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines whether large vision-language models can protect privacy according to rules that users specify in language at inference time. The authors introduce SPY-Bench, with 32,700 image-question samples and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 scenarios, along with metrics based on user specifications and context awareness. Testing 21 models, most achieved only about 24% compliance accuracy, and the authors report a Noise Contrastive Alignment variant reaching 96.88% accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce inference-time personalized privacy protection, build a 32,700-sample benchmark, evaluate 21 LVLMs, and propose a contrastive alignment variant.

entry.title: Pulse or Provenance? Checking What rPPG Deepfake Detectors Actually Learn
entry.summary: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines whether rPPG-based deepfake detectors rely on genuine heart-rate signals. Controlled experiments on Celeb-DF++ and FaceForensics++ indicate the detectors mainly pick up on video source characteristics rather than physiological pulse. The authors also report that official Celeb-DF splits share identities and source videos between training and test sets. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show rPPG detectors learn video provenance and high-frequency artifacts rather than physiology, using controlled experiments on Celeb-DF++ and FF++, a caution for evaluation.

entry.title: Neuron-level study of how Mixture-of-Experts language models specialize by domain
entry.summary: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines how domain specialization is organized inside Mixture-of-Experts language models, looking below the expert level to individual neurons. The authors introduce Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP) to identify domain-specialized neurons and trace how their importance changes during pre-training and post-training. They also propose RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr), which at 75% neuron retention preserves 91-98% of original performance across six models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose neuron-level MoE specialization analysis and RAMP-based pruning, tracing training across three MoE families and reporting results on six models.

entry.title: Counterfactual analysis of lesion extent leakage from annotation-derived prompts in vision-language medical image segmentation
entry.summary: Counterfactual Analysis of Extent Leakage from Annotation-Derived Prompts in Vision-Language Medical Image Segmentation arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines text-guided medical image segmentation, where captions about lesions improve accuracy. On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, the gains come mainly from lesion extent words such as size or lung-zone phrases, which were computed from the evaluation masks, a effect the authors call extent leakage. Counterfactual experiments keeping or removing these words support the finding. The authors also propose an evaluation protocol that separates information about the image from information copied from the label. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show annotation-derived captions leak lesion extent, testing this via counterfactual ablations and retraining across colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and chest X-ray, with implications for e

entry.title: PARDIG: Global Rain Estimates Learned from Sparse Satellite Data
entry.summary: PARDIG: Global Precipitation Estimates Learned from Sparse Satellite Observations arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper presents PARDIG, an AI framework using a spherical graph-mesh transformer that produces near-real-time global precipitation estimates. It is trained on atmospheric analyses and geostationary satellite imagery to predict sparse, high-precision spaceborne radar measurements, then applied globally at 0.1° and 15-minute resolution. Evaluations against radar networks and surface stations show it outperforms IMERG, MSWEP, ERA5, and HRES, with the largest gains at extreme intensities. Both historical and near-real-time datasets are openly released under CC BY 4.0. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a spherical graph-mesh transformer trained on sparse spaceborne radar that outperforms IMERG, MSWEP, and ERA5 against radar networks and over 36,000 surface stations.

entry.title: Best-possible final-iterate error bounds for a stochastic fixed-point method
entry.summary: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper proves mean-square residual bounds for the last iterate of stochastic approximation with nonexpansive maps, also called stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann iterations, using polynomially decaying stepsizes. It studies three noise conditions and gives bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. Unlike contractive stochastic approximation, square-summable stepsizes are shown to be necessary in the nonexpansive setting. The framework is applied to stochastic gradient descent, linear stochastic approximation, and learning in cocoercive games. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation under three noise conditions, reporting tight bounds up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: Fairly splitting LLM batch energy among requests using Shapley values
entry.summary: Scaling Shapley Energy Attribution to Large LLM Batches arXiv · Nov 10, 2026LLM serving engines batch requests, and GPUs report only total energy, so providers need a fair way to assign energy to each request for billing. This paper proposes StepSplit, which splits each inference step's energy into a shared part and a request-specific part to derive a closed-form Shapley value. It works for both static and continuous batching, with a correction for the latter. Evaluated against Shapley values from 529,513 GPU runs, StepSplit's error is far lower than token-proportional allocation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a closed-form Shapley energy split with a replay correction for continuous batching, reporting L1 errors of 0.4-6.4% against measured Shapley values from 529,513 GPU runs.

entry.title: LLM validation of minimal-pair language tests makes them easier for the models tested
entry.summary: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper examines whether large language models can replace costly human judgments for validating minimal-pair benchmarks such as BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French). It finds that LLM-based filtering removes items that language models fail but humans do not, so the remaining items are easier for the models being tested. The authors release code, validator outputs and item-level scores. ★★★★ Notable: The authors test LLM validation of minimal-pair benchmarks against human panels, reporting that filtering makes items easier for models across BLiMP, QFrBLiMP and BLiMP-NL.

entry.title: Selecting Feature Interactions by Checking Whether They Replicate Across Independent Models
entry.summary: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper introduces LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions. It trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions, removing main effects to measure each feature pair's interaction strength. It tests whether the second model reproduces the pattern at a meaningful strength, using a single multiple-testing correction and only two model fits. Experiments on synthetic designs, French motor insurance data, and two credit datasets show it retains few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors select feature interactions via independent replication, prove a strength floor restores selection consistency, and report results on synthetic and real data.

entry.title: Recursive memory for prediction and generation: a theory paper on why memory needs differ sharply between predicting and generating
entry.summary: Recursive memory for prediction and generation arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies how recurrent and state-space language models compress the past into a fixed-size state. For a known hidden Markov source, about O(log(1/ε)) bits suffice to answer any question about the future to accuracy ε, because the Bayesian filter forgets rounding errors. When sampled tokens are fed back into the state, however, generating T tokens can require on the order of log(T/ε) bits, a lower bound derived from the KL chain rule. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show generating futures needs log(T/ε)-bit state versus constant-size for prediction, with a lower bound via KL chain rule, tight for two-state sources.

entry.title: Deterministic, reproducible AI inference using exact integer arithmetic, enabling verifiable distributed inference
entry.summary: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper presents tritify, an open-source runtime that runs model inference entirely in exact integer arithmetic, using floating point only for offline quantization and verification. The authors report bit-identical outputs across CPUs, instruction sets and CPU/GPU, decision agreement with a float reference, and identical results when computation is split across multiple machines. From this they argue that distributed inference can be verified by re-deriving the exact output bytes, though protection against a dishonest server is left to future work. ★★★★ Notable: The authors run real models' forward passes in exact integer arithmetic, report bit-identical outputs across hardware and machines, and validate on several models including a 106B MoE.

entry.title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans: GenEA, a model that infers people's goals and multi-step plans from their actions
entry.summary: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper introduces GenEA, an agent representation for reasoning about multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. It extends task-and-motion planning with simulation-based intuitive physics, coupling an articulated body's coarse biomechanics with its interactions with nearby objects. Embedding this state-space in a generative model yields a joint distribution over goals and embodied plans. In object manipulation and navigation experiments, GenEA recapitulates human reasoning about embodied plans and outperforms heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build a generative model over goals and embodied plans, comparing it to heuristics, task-and-motion planning, and a vision-language model in manipulation and navigation experiments.

entry.title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
entry.summary: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper introduces CP-MLPs, a tensor framework that treats each multiplicative unit as a rank-1 interaction with detector, value, and output roles. It proves exact tensor-rank separations between tied gated blocks such as ReLU² and untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU, showing the width advantage of untying depends on the target structure. Experiments indicate that loss plateaus alone do not establish an approximation gap, since arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use CP tensor rank to show exact separations between tied and untied gated MLP blocks, with width advantages depending on target structure.

entry.title: Third-order asymptotics for fixed-length lossy compression of discrete sources
entry.summary: Third-Order Asymptotics for Fixed-Length Lossy Compression of Discrete Memoryless Sources arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper determines the third-order asymptotics of the logarithm of the minimum codebook size for fixed-length lossy compression of discrete memoryless sources. For every interior distortion level under an excess-distortion probability constraint, it establishes a third-order correction of (1/2)log n + O(1), where n is the blocklength. The result sharpens general bounds by Kostina and Verdú (2012). The main technical contribution is the converse for positive dispersion, proved with a multivariate weighted-strip estimate. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a tight third-order asymptotic for lossy codebook size, improving Kostina and Verdú via a reverse change of measure.

entry.title: Proof that pair-merge tokenisation is hard to approximate on binary strings and strongly NP-hard on unary datasets
entry.summary: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies how tokenisers such as BPE shorten text by repeatedly merging adjacent symbol pairs. The authors prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve an approximation within a factor of about n/log n, even for a single binary string. For merges that may skip occurrences, they give a simple algorithm achieving O(n/log log n). Over a one-letter alphabet, the related tokenisation problems are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce BPE-style merge selection to grammar size, proving approximation hardness on binary strings and strong NP-completeness for unary datasets.

entry.title: Adaptive catalyst discovery via composable AI for catalysis
entry.summary: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper presents Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders reusable by task-specific models. On benchmark tasks it achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. Experimentally, it identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst for industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of a commercial benchmark, and guided closed-loop optimization of a Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling that outperformed traditional Ni-based systems. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a modular catalyst AI framework with reusable physicochemical encoders, reporting benchmark gains and two experimental validations in catalyst discovery.

entry.title: Simultaneously Identifying Near-Optimal Regions in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
entry.summary: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper studies how to identify, on a continuous design space, the regions of near-optimal designs for all tolerances up to a maximum T, with region estimation error at most η. It gives a lower bound on the number of simulation evaluations any procedure requires. It proposes SASORI, which returns an optimal point estimate and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formulate simultaneous near-optimal region identification across all tolerances, derive a minimax lower bound, and report an algorithm matching it up to log factors.

entry.title: Exact sample requirements for learning KL-regularized reinforcement learning policies
entry.summary: Sharp Sample Complexity of KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies how many samples are needed to learn policies in KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback. For discounted MDPs, it shows that a plug-in estimator reaches an epsilon-optimal policy with a stated sample bound, and that no algorithm can do better under certain conditions. The authors also derive the exact asymptotic constant of the estimator and an optimal sample allocation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give tight sample complexity bounds for KL-regularized RL, improving the H^5 horizon dependence and adding a temperature-dependent lower bound, checked by simulations on small MDPs.

entry.title: A zero-cost uncertainty measure for LLM outputs, derived from particle decoding
entry.summary: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level Rényi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper shows that Sequential Monte Carlo decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which yields a sequence-level Rényi entropy for an LLM's completions at essentially no extra cost. It proves that orders above one relate to each step's most likely token, while the order-1/2 entropy accumulates per-step search effort, and reports this as the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 it outperforms log-probability in AUROC, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy with 34.2% fewer particles. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive sequence-level Rényi entropy from SMC power-sampling normalizers at zero extra cost, with a chain rule; the abstract reports AUROC gains over log-probability on MATH500 and a two-pa

entry.title: Bursts That Keep Hurting: Persistent Slowdown in Prefix-Cached LLM Agent Serving
entry.summary: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies a failure mode in serving LLM agents with prefix caching, where a brief burst of extra requests pushes a server into a degraded state for a long time, with low cache hit ratio, about half throughput, and a growing backlog. A matched server without the burst stays healthy. The authors give a workload-balance condition for when the degraded state can drain, find that throttling new admissions helps little, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity limit recovers service within minutes. A budgeter that bounds active sessions' resident KV demand to the cache pool prevented the failure in all tested runs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a metastable degradation in prefix-cached agent serving after bursts and a KV-budgeting method that prevented it in tested runs.

entry.title: Optimal Constant in One-Shot Channel Simulation and Strong Functional Representation
entry.summary: The Optimal Constant for One-Shot Channel Simulation and Strong Functional Representation Lemma arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper proves a tight bound for one-shot channel simulation by strengthening the strong functional representation lemma. For random variables X and Y, it constructs a variable Z with I(Z;X)=H(Y|X,Z)=0 and bounds H(Y|Z) in terms of the mutual information I, showing the constant term is optimal. The paper also shows Poisson functional representation is nearly optimal up to a constant gap and gives a finite-blocklength achievability bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a tight bound for one-shot channel simulation with an optimal constant term, a notable theoretical improvement over prior strong functional representation results.

entry.title: How Hyperbolic Are Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models?
entry.summary: How Hyperbolic Are Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models? arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines whether the exponential map, which introduces hyperbolic curvature, meaningfully affects hyperbolic vision-language models. The authors find that across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP the map is approximated well by the identity, and removing it at inference leaves scores unchanged. Euclidean models trained on CC3M under the same hierarchy losses match the hyperbolic counterparts in statistics, evaluation scores, and radial distributions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors question hyperbolic VLMs by analyzing the exponential map and report matching results with Euclidean models trained on CC3M.

entry.title: Closing the burn-in gap: tight risk bounds for averaged SGD in linear regression
entry.summary: Settling the Burn-in Gap: Sharp Risk Bounds for Tail-Averaged SGD in Linear Regression arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies the excess risk of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression. Building on Zou et al. (2021), it gives matching upper and lower bounds on total excess risk under a trajectory spectral feedback condition, and shows that both existing bounds are loose. The authors prove the condition holds in two constant-stepsize regimes and provide one- and two-dimensional constructions showing an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the earlier lower bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give matching tail-averaged SGD bounds closing a gap in Zou et al. (2021), plus one- and two-dimensional separation constructions.

entry.title: Enforcing Fairness Axioms in Loss-Based AI Alignment
entry.summary: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies whether reward models trained on pairwise comparisons, as in RLHF, respect Pareto optimality (PO), treating each principle as a voter. It shows PO can still fail for polynomial reward models and one-hidden-layer ReLU MLPs. Under idealized conditions with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths, PO can be recovered for linear rewards, motivating dataset design as a remedy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model constitutional principles as voters and show loss-trained polynomial and one-hidden-layer MLP rewards can violate Pareto optimality, recovering it in an idealized linear setting.

entry.title: A proof that no finite rulebook can certify every safe AI-generated program
entry.summary: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper asks whether a gatekeeper can decide from code alone which AI-written programs may run, given rules that must be backed by finite, machine-checkable evidence. It proves that complete allow and deny rulebooks are impossible: prohibitions can only be caught when violated, never cleared for good, while confidentiality and responsiveness cannot be settled either way. The authors also show that a sound rulebook of n bits omits a compliant program of about n bits, and they offer a weaker guarantee: a checkable list that includes all required allowances and excludes all refusals. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove finite checkable evidence cannot certify all safe programs, characterize confidentiality and responsiveness rules, and bound rulebook size.

entry.title: Preventing Adversarial Attacks from Transferring to Fine-Tuned Speech Recognition Models
entry.summary: TransferBreaker: Breaking Adversarial Transferability in Fine-Tuned Speech Recognition arXiv · Oct 7, 2026Many organizations fine-tune public pretrained speech recognition models and deploy them as black boxes, assuming limited access offers protection. This paper shows that adversarial perturbations crafted on the public base model transfer effectively to fine-tuned models, severely degrading performance. The authors propose TransferBreaker, a fine-tuning framework combining three components to suppress adversarial transfer. Evaluated across three languages and four large ASR models, it reduces adversarial word error rate from 92.6 to 27.8. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose TransferBreaker, a fine-tuning framework with theory that reportedly cuts adversarial WER from 92.6 to 27.8 across three languages and four large ASR models.

entry.title: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits
entry.summary: Quantized memory of measurement records near the light cone of quantum circuits arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper studies the statistics of mid-circuit measurement outcomes in quantum circuits and shows they become exactly solvable near the light cone. In brickwork circuits, measurements along the light-cone edge form a two-state Markov chain, and the memory of the record is quantized to at most one bit per site of displacement. The authors also present a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity and test the predictions on a 156-qubit superconducting processor. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show measurement-record memory near the light cone is exactly solvable and quantized, and report verification on a 156-qubit processor.

entry.title: Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing: how disorder-induced modes in conductors cause correlated qubit dephasing
entry.summary: Long-range correlated quantum errors from diffuson-correlated dephasing arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper shows that low-energy disorder-induced modes called diffusons in a diffusive conductor cause spatially correlated dephasing on qubits sharing that conductor. Using a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model, the authors derive the noise kernel in closed form, which decays as the inverse square of qubit separation and changes sign with pair orientation. In two dimensions, the worst-case correlated noise a qubit shares with an array grows logarithmically with array size, so standard fault-tolerance threshold conditions may no longer hold for large arrays. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose diffuson-correlated dephasing, derive a closed-form noise kernel, and argue it can violate fault-tolerance threshold conditions in large arrays.

entry.title: Rational quantum spectral filters via a repeat-until-success protocol
entry.summary: Rational quantum spectral filtering by repeat-until-success protocol arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper introduces a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, going beyond the polynomial transformations of QSP and QSVT. The protocol interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator with mid-circuit measurements. The authors exactly characterize which spectral filters can be realized upon acceptance and give a constructive compiler with memory and query-cost bounds. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy show query-cost advantages over a fixed-depth QSVT baseline. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a finite-memory repeat-until-success protocol to realize rational spectral filters beyond QSP/QSVT polynomials, with an exact characterization, compiler, and reported query-cost compar

entry.title: FusionQ: A General Optimal Decoder for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
entry.summary: FusionQ: A Generic and Optimal Decoding Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction arXiv · Nov 10, 2026FusionQ is a decoding framework for quantum error correction that builds small local decoding problems around clusters of triggered detectors, rather than solving one large global problem. It expands a local problem only when its best solution uses virtual boundary errors, and then merges the local results into a single global correction. The authors prove that, with an exact minimum-weight local solver, the fused result equals the global most-likely error solution of the original model. Evaluations report that the exact-backend version matches the monolithic result on every shot and reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with syndrome acquisition. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a fusion framework with a compositional optimality theorem matching global MLE, and report latency reductions across decoder backends.

entry.title: An improved (1+2e)-approximation algorithm for metric data placement
entry.summary: An Improved (1+2e)-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies the metric data placement problem, which involves placing resources at sites with capacity limits and fixed installation costs to minimize total placement and access costs. The authors present a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm built on a linear programming relaxation, using multiscale metric-ball partitions and a min-cost circulation. By optimizing ball radii, they achieve an approximation factor of 1+2e (about 6.44), the best known guarantee for this problem since its introduction in 2001. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a deterministic polynomial-time 1+2e approximation for metric data placement, improving the 2001 bound via LP relaxation and a flow network.

entry.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Measuring Dollar Totals with AI Labels and Limited Human Review
entry.summary: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies how AI tools can help measure monetary totals across many administrative records when human readers disagree on labels. The testbed uses 121,070 US tax-filing grant-purpose texts covering 799,675 records, labelled by a rule-based classifier, three language models, and three independent human readers. It proposes estimators and two rules for accepting machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, and finds that a two-phase human review policy lowers the total's RMSE by 28% at a budget of 100 texts. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine dollar-weighted measurement, selective machine labelling and budgeted human review, giving exact conditions and cross-fitting; they report simulations and replay on 121,070 tax-fil

entry.title: X Marks the Spot: Diffusion Models for Photo Location Prediction Using Location Embeddings
entry.summary: X Marks the Spot: Diffusion for Image Geolocalization with Location Representations arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper addresses image geolocalization, which predicts where a photo was taken. Instead of generating coordinates directly, the authors learn in the representation space of a pretrained location encoder, using a Location Autoencoder that maps embeddings back to coordinates. They train DIG, a latent diffusion model that generates location embeddings conditioned on image features. The paper reports that DIG outperforms coordinate-based generative models and sets a new state of the art for parametric geolocalization on OSV-5M, Im2GPS3k, and YFCC4k. ★★★★ Notable: The authors diffuse in pretrained location-encoder embedding space rather than generating coordinates, reporting new state-of-the-art parametric results on three benchmarks.

entry.title: How much a partial view of a toric-code qubit leaks, and the Nishimori point
entry.summary: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper studies how much information a partial observer can learn about a logical bit in a fault-tolerant quantum computer by accessing only some of its qubits. It proves that, for any region and any Pauli noise, the observer's best advantage equals 1 minus twice the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. It also links the operational threshold of a two-row strip to the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the eavesdropper advantage equals 1-2P_fail for any region and Pauli noise, linking strip thresholds to the Nishimori point and testing on IBM hardware.

entry.title: An AI agent autonomously optimizes numerical algorithms for atomistic simulation
entry.summary: Autonomous Optimization of Numerical Algorithms by an AI Agent: Application to Atomistic Simulation arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper presents AIOA, a framework where a large-language-model coding agent improves atomistic simulation algorithms in a loop protected by verifiers it cannot change. Applied to the ASE library, agents made six kernels about 22 to 24 times faster on average in Python while keeping results unchanged. On unseen problems, the agents' optimizers needed 3.1 to 3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6 to 17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band for reaction paths. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply LLM coding agents in an improvement loop to atomistic simulation algorithms, reporting two components absent from the literature and several-fold fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS

entry.title: Left-side ripple effects in byte-pair encoding: certified lookbehind for any dictionary
entry.summary: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper builds on Berglund and van der Merwe's formalization of byte-pair encoding and studies how far a prepended string on the left can change a tokenization. It gives a method that applies to every dictionary, deciding the origin radius in polynomial time and characterizing when it is infinite. The authors also present a streaming tokenizer that emits tokens no continuation can change, and report results for the merge tables of GPT-2, cl100k, o200k and Llama 3. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve the open left-prepend question for BPE, deciding infinite radius for all dictionaries and reporting infinite origin radius for GPT-2, cl100k, o200k and Llama 3.

entry.title: Code-grounded AI agent explanations for static analysis security findings
entry.summary: Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings arXiv · Nov 9, 2026The paper presents SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that uses a large language model to explain vulnerabilities reported by static analysis tools, while detection remains with the analyser. The model is an agent that must consult the repository and the rule that fired before answering. In a within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants, the redesign raised System Usability Scale scores from 77.3 to 85.0 and made a correct remediation 2.6 times more likely. Triage accuracy and time per finding showed no clear difference, and trust did not change. ★★★★ Notable: Keeps detection with the analyser and uses a repository-consulting agent for explanations; a 24-participant crossover study reports SUS rising from 77.3 to 85.0 and 2.6x higher odds of correct remedia

entry.title: Open Browser-Based Implementation Flow for Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, Byte-Checked Against ISE
entry.summary: An Open Implementation Flow for the Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 that Runs in the Browser, Checked Byte for Byte Against ISE arXiv · Nov 9, 2026This paper presents an open implementation flow that takes designs from HDL to a programmable bitstream for Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 devices, which the discontinued ISE 14.7 supports. The flow runs in a web browser or Node.js using Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly. For the same placed and routed design, the bitstream is byte-identical to the one written by ISE's bitgen, and ISE's DRC is clean. The flow is published as the npm package silinx-fpga under Apache-2.0. ★★★★ Notable: The authors integrate nextpnr with measured Spartan-3E/6 bit data to run in browser; the paper reports byte-identical bitstreams versus ISE and comparisons on 67 designs.

entry.title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Arithmetic Geometry in Language Models
entry.summary: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models arXiv · Nov 8, 2026This paper studies geometric shapes found in the activations of large language models, asking whether they reflect how the model actually computes. It argues that probe accuracy alone cannot establish this and proposes a four-stage Bayesian pipeline testing decodability, shape, ownership, and causal use separately. Tested on two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Pythia 6.9B, nearly all concepts are decodable, but decoded directions overlap substantially across concepts. The authors suggest reporting probe results as verdicts on all four claims rather than a single accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors split probe accuracy into four claims and test them with a Bayesian pipeline on three LLMs, reporting that most shapes are inherited rather than owned.

entry.title: Exploration via Exploitation: Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
entry.summary: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL arXiv · Nov 7, 2026This paper studies personalized federated reinforcement learning, treating differing agent rewards as a structural asset that promotes exploration rather than an obstacle to consensus. It proposes PF-UCBVI, which decouples shared dynamics from personalized objectives to achieve optimal linear speedup. It also introduces PF-EFVI, a purely greedy algorithm without explicit exploration bonuses, which attains logarithmic regret under sufficient reward diversity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast reward heterogeneity as an exploration asset and report a logarithmic regret bound for a purely greedy federated algorithm.

entry.title: Using Predictive Surprise to Build an Interpretable, Self-Grounded Time-Series Classifier
entry.summary: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series arXiv · Nov 7, 2026This paper introduces ConceptTime, which uses a frozen probabilistic forecaster to compute predictive surprise at each timestep, using it both to locate segment boundaries and to summarize each segment. These summaries are clustered into a vocabulary of dynamical-regime concepts, and a lightweight head classifies sequences from this concept sequence. The distance to the nearest concept provides a reliability measure, and the authors report competitive accuracy across 17 public benchmarks without annotations. ★★★★ Notable: Uses predictive surprise to segment time series and build concepts without annotations; the authors report evaluation on 17 public benchmarks.

entry.title: AI governance should focus on control and knowledge limits, not just capping intelligence.
entry.summary: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper proposes a "competence circuit" framework (IKC + KC + C) that splits an AI agent's real-world impact into intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. It tests this framework against the fast-takeoff debate using stochastic simulations on NK fitness landscapes. The authors argue that the main safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an IKC+KC+C framework, formalize fast takeoff as a conjunction, and report simulations on NK landscapes with an analytic speedup bound.

entry.title: Quadratic Randomized Encodings for All Functions with Statistical Privacy
entry.summary: From Degree Three to Degree Two: Statistical Randomized Encodings for All Functions IACR ePrint · Nov 7, 2026The paper constructs quadratic randomized encodings for every Boolean function, with exponentially small correctness and statistical privacy errors. The encoding, decoder and simulator have complexity polynomial in the size of mod-2 branching programs and the security parameter. The results extend to multiparty encodings and yield applications such as one-way functions of output locality three and non-interactive client-server protocols. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report quadratic statistical randomized encodings for every Boolean function with exponentially small errors, answering the open degree-two and locality-three questions and extending to mu

entry.title: More Keys, Less Commitment: Key-Committing Attacks on BBB Accordions and a New Transform
entry.summary: More Keys, Less Commitment: Key-Committing Attacks on BBB Accordions via Encode-then-Encipher and a Key-Committing Transform IACR ePrint · Nov 7, 2026This paper examines whether beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security of cryptographic accordions strengthens key commitment in authenticated encryption built from them. It shows that extra keys introduced for BBB security give adversaries additional freedom, enabling O(1) key-committing attacks on many schemes, mostly built via Encode-then-Encipher. The authors propose CACH, a black-box transform from BBB-secure accordions to robust authenticated encryption with key-committing security, instantiated with CHCTR2. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show extra keys in BBB accordions enable O(1) key-committing attacks on several AE schemes and propose the CACH transform, with reported security bounds and performance comparisons.

entry.title: Removing padding in cryptography by proving the hardness of certifying random strings
entry.summary: Overcoming Padding in Cryptography via Hardness of Certifying Random Strings IACR ePrint · Nov 7, 2026Many cryptographic security proofs use hybrid arguments whose intermediate descriptions are larger than the real scheme, forcing the real scheme to be artificially padded. This superfluous padding blocks succinct primitives whose parameter sizes do not grow with input length. The paper introduces a framework that removes padding by linking cryptography to proof complexity through proof-complexity generators (PCGs). Its master theorem lifts security on compressible instances to all instances when PCGs exist. Applications include rate-1 iO, succinct witness encryption, succinct non-interactive arguments with short CRS for NP subclasses, and multi-input functional encryption for unbounded arity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link cryptography and proof complexity via PCGs to eliminate padding, reporting applications to rate-1 iO and succinct witness encryption.

entry.title: Round-optimal statistical verifiable secret sharing with polynomial cost
entry.summary: Round-Optimal Statistical Verifiable Secret Sharing with Polynomial Complexity IACR ePrint · Nov 7, 2026This paper studies verifiable secret sharing (VSS), a cryptographic primitive that keeps secret distribution and reconstruction correct even when some participants are corrupt. Earlier work by Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra achieved round optimality but with communication exponential in the number of parties. This paper presents the first round-optimal statistical VSS for t<n/2 with polynomial communication and computation. The protocol is built from a new notion of weak secret sharing. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give the first round-optimal statistical VSS with polynomial communication and computation for t<n/2, via a new weak secret sharing notion.

entry.title: Minimum bucket size for reliable Path ORAM, a memory-access-hiding method
entry.summary: The Minimum Bucket Capacity for Reliable Path ORAM IACR ePrint · Nov 8, 2026Path ORAM hides memory access patterns by storing data blocks in a binary tree with buckets of capacity Z, and keeping blocks that do not fit in a client-side stash. The paper shows that Z=4 is the smallest bucket capacity giving a uniform exponential bound on stash overflow probability for binary Path ORAM. For Z=3, it constructs instances where a single sequential scan of all blocks produces a stash of size Ω(N) with probability bounded away from zero.'] ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report a uniform exponential stash bound at Z=4 and a linear lower bound at Z=3, giving a sharp threshold via an auxiliary independent-geometric model.

entry.title: Re-examining the Security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF
entry.summary: Revisiting the Security of OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF IACR ePrint · Nov 8, 2026This paper revisits the security of the online authenticated encryption schemes OleF, t-OleF, and OlÆF and identifies two independent flaws. It shows a mask-compensation relation between continuation and termination processing in OleF and t-OleF, which enables a two-query distinguisher against OleF and a similar attack on t-OleF using concrete AXU hash families. The attacks are extended to OlÆF, breaking its privacy and integrity. The paper also refutes a claimed ideal integrity bound for variable-expansion online authenticated encryption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a mask-compensation relation in OleF and construct a two-query distinguisher, and report counterexamples refuting an ideal RUP bound.

entry.title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle-Aided Computation: Short Proofs for AI Tasks That Use External Information
entry.summary: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation IACR ePrint · Nov 9, 2026This paper studies incrementally verifiable computation (IVC), which lets a prover keep a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step without re-running earlier steps. Under the Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption, the authors construct IVC schemes for oracle-aided computations, which depend on external information and human judgment. They give privately verifiable constructions for robust computations and publicly verifiable constructions for oracles that sign their answers, and also prove a lower bound for certain publicly verifiable schemes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend IVC to oracle-aided computation, giving LWE-based constructions in robust and signed-oracle settings plus a lower bound.

entry.title: A paper on critical properties of EPR steering, a quantum entanglement effect
entry.summary: Critical properties of EPR steering arXiv · Nov 6, 2026This paper studies EPR steering, a phenomenon in quantum entanglement where one party's measurements can influence another party's conditional states. The authors prove that every PVM-critical entangled two-qubit state becomes steerable when two copies are available. They show that measurement entanglement, the number of measurements, and collective access each play different roles in revealing steering. The paper also constructs higher-dimensional states whose two-copy steering violation is unbounded, answering the amplification question posed by Hsieh, Liang, and Lee affirmatively. ★★★★ Notable: The authors claim every PVM-critical two-qubit entangled state becomes steerable with two copies, identifying a critical threshold where measurement entanglement vanishes, and report unbounded two-cop

entry.title: Can price-impact decay be statistically identified through propagator estimation? Diffusive prices make the inferred kernel transient and fine-tuned
entry.summary: Is price-impact decay statistically identifiable by propagator estimation? Diffusive prices force the inferred kernel to be transient and fine-tuned arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper proves a no-go theorem showing that the asymptotic decay of price impact cannot be statistically identified by propagator estimation under long-memory order flow, because diffusive prices return a fine-tuned decay even when true impact is permanent. Using universal Wiener–Hopf deconvolution results, the authors show the inferred propagator is necessarily transient and, under a mild condition, decays with an exponent fixed by order-flow autocorrelation alone. They illustrate this with an exactly solvable null model whose true impact is strictly permanent, yet whose inferred propagator displays an artificial fine-tuned decay. ★★★★ Notable: The authors argue that propagator estimation cannot identify price-impact decay: under long-memory order flow the inferred kernel is transient with a fine-tuned decay even when true impact is permanen

entry.title: Clinical Data's Dark Matter: Limits on Separating Physiology from Care Process in EHRs
entry.summary: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records arXiv · Nov 9, 2026This paper argues that representations learned from electronic health records mix patient physiology with the clinical process that determines what is measured, when, and for whom. The authors formalize the data-generating process and analyze two strategies for separating these components. They show that a single dataset cannot identify how information from laboratory values and orderings is divided, and that cross-site invariance tests are falsifiable hypotheses rather than identification methods. Identification becomes possible under certain conditions, such as when tests are performed for every patient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize EHR data generation and argue that physiology and care process cannot be separated from a single dataset, offering a falsifiable cross-site invariance test; their worked example

entry.title: Paper on letting a frozen model learn robot manipulation tasks in context within a simulated world
entry.summary: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper proposes World In-Context Learning (WICL), in which a frozen model learns from one demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes feedback into its context rather than its weights. The authors build RoboScript to implement this for robot manipulation. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, it reports 83.4% mean success, which they say exceeds the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose WICL, learning manipulation in context via simulated rehearsal, reporting 83.4% mean success on 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks from one demonstration, over 20 points above trained policies.

entry.title: Simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing: the device size at which exact classical sampling becomes too slow
entry.summary: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper proposes the time a classical computer needs to draw one exact sample from a photonic device's output distribution as a common unit for comparing when such devices outgrow classical simulation. It defines the simulability frontier as the device size at which the fastest exact sampler yields one sample per second on a fixed machine. Using photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library, the authors measure frontiers on one NVIDIA H100 GPU: 38.3 single photons, 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter, and 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose exact per-sample sampling time as a common unit and report frontier values for several light sources.

entry.title: An efficient classical algorithm for estimating OTOCs in chaotic quantum circuits
entry.summary: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper presents a polynomial-time classical algorithm for estimating four-point and eight-point out-of-time-ordered correlators in typical one-dimensional random quantum circuits. It exploits dephasing caused by quantum chaos to suppress subleading terms in a rapidly converging series. At larger circuit depths, the authors report higher signal-to-noise ratio than recent 2D experiments by Google. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a polynomial-time classical algorithm for OTOCs in 1D random circuits, exploiting chaos-induced dephasing; numerical results are compared with Google's 2D experiments.

entry.title: Comparing Sequential and Parallel Ways to Share Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
entry.summary: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies two experimentally feasible ways of sharing a quantum system among several observers, parallel and sequential sharing, to extract encoded information. With two observers, any statistics from parallel sharing can be reproduced sequentially, but with more observers some parallel statistics cannot be. The authors show that quantum advantage cannot be shared in parallel for a class of tasks with two decoding measurements, and discuss 3-bit random access codes, where parallel sharing becomes possible in the parity-oblivious variant. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show parallel and sequential sharing are equivalent for two observers but differ for more, with arbitrarily large gaps.

entry.title: Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements: adding completion qubits so local checks commute, enabling fault-tolerant logical measurement
entry.summary: Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements arXiv · Nov 9, 2026The paper introduces completion qubits that make local checks commute for Clifford Z2 symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes, adding one per noncommuting pair while preserving the gauged code space, its distance, and the Clifford property of the checks. It extends the approach to qudits and shows that gauging and ungauging a distance-d code implements a logical measurement with circuit fault distance Ω(d) in O(d) rounds. The construction is demonstrated by gauging two toric codes into the D(D4) quantum double and back. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce completion qubits that make gauging checks commute, preserving distance and Clifford structure, with circuit fault distance Omega(d) for logical measurement.

entry.title: Testing whether gravity's phase dynamics are quantum under strong noise
entry.summary: Testing non-classical gravitational phase dynamics under strong dephasing arXiv · Nov 9, 2026The paper asks whether gravity must be quantum by examining its phase dynamics rather than entanglement, which noise often destroys. Within a dephased Bose–Marletto–Vedral setup, the authors prove an exact finite-time difference between gravitational conditional-phase evolution and any passive stochastic local-phase model driven by a classical mediator. The distinction persists, with modified sensitivity, when population-preserving classical measurement and feedback are included. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report an exact finite-time criterion separating gravitational conditional-phase dynamics from passive stochastic local-phase models under strong dephasing, extended to classical measureme

entry.title: A universal fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture using globally driven atom arrays
entry.summary: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays arXiv · Nov 9, 2026This paper proposes a universal fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture based on globally driven dual-species atom arrays. Qubits are selected through interspecies Rydberg interactions in a hybrid neutral-atom system, avoiding locally addressed quantum gates. The authors define a native instruction set, GRAIL, into which surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation are compiled, and report an error-correction threshold of 1.43% for the resulting quantum memory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a globally driven dual-species atom architecture with a native instruction set, reporting a 1.43% threshold under a hardware-inferred noise model.

entry.title: Proof of the QNEC without extra assumptions, using a weight
entry.summary: Proof of the QNEC, without assumptions and under a weight arXiv · Nov 9, 2026The paper completes a proof of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) within the half-sided translations and modular inclusions framework, removing an assumption required by earlier proofs. It establishes that the relative entropy between the state of fields outside a stationary black hole and a Hartle-Hawking state is always a convex function of the horizon cut. The authors also present a generalization of the QNEC in which the Hartle-Hawking Hilbert space is replaced by one built on a weight. ★★★★ Notable: The authors remove an assumption from prior QNEC proofs and generalize the result to a weight-based Hilbert space.

entry.title: Proof of the Rényi QNEC
entry.summary: Proof of the Rényi QNEC arXiv · Nov 9, 2026This paper proves the Rényi version of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC). The proof uses Araki-Masuda weighted L_p norms for all p > 2 and generalizes the algebraic proof for p=2. The authors also examine properties of the corresponding weighted conditional entropy. The p=2 limit corresponds to a conditional dynamical entropy originally defined in black hole dynamics. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the algebraic QNEC proof to Rényi versions for all p>2 using weighted conditional Lp norms.

entry.title: Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions
entry.summary: Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions arXiv · Nov 9, 2026This paper proves a Lieb-Robinson bound (LRB), which describes an approximate causal structure in quantum many-body dynamics, for a standard system of one-dimensional continuum fermions. Previously such bounds were established only for quantum spin systems and certain lattice boson systems. The result applies to initial states with controlled local particle number and energy moments, and is therefore thermodynamically stable. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions, for initial states with controlled local particle number and energy moments.

entry.title: Unbounded benefit of adaptive quantum measurements in entanglement-assisted communication
entry.summary: Unbounded advantage of adaptivity in entanglement-assisted communication arXiv · Nov 8, 2026This paper studies how shared entanglement can cut the classical communication needed for distributed computation. It shows tasks that adaptive protocols solve with just three messages, while non-adaptive quantum receivers need unboundedly many. The authors also prove two complementary limits relating adaptive and non-adaptive protocols. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the advantage of adaptivity in entanglement-assisted communication is unbounded and give two complementary simulation limits.

entry.title: Quantum circuits cannot exactly simulate the quantum switch
entry.summary: Simulating the quantum switch with quantum circuits is impossible arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The quantum switch is a higher-order operation that combines input quantum channels in an indefinite causal order. The paper proves that no quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate it for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls. The result already holds for qubit channels and extends to the complete r-switch, which controls all permutations of r input channels. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order cannot exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch, extending to the complete r-switch.

entry.title: Estimating Linear-Optical Amplitudes with Entangled Inputs
entry.summary: On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper studies how to estimate output amplitudes of a linear-optical interferometer when the input photons are entangled. The authors give an unbiased estimator whose mean-square error falls as 1/N with the number of draws, regardless of the interferometer, output pattern, or entanglement. It applies to inputs that are matrix-product states of bounded bond dimension, such as light from sequential quantum emitters. The guarantees are additive, and the method also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and marginals. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend unbiased amplitude estimation to entangled matrix-product-state inputs, giving an interferometer-independent mean-square error bound and polynomial cost for sequential quantum-emitt

entry.title: Trace adds one quantifier: exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games
entry.summary: A trace costs one quantifier: the exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper asks whether players of a finite nonlocal game can win with certainty, meaning a perfect strategy exists. It proves that for normal spatial strategies this existence question is Σ⁰₂-complete, so it stays undecidable even with a halting-problem oracle, which is harder than the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models. The authors also show that requiring finite trace adds one existential number quantifier, and several related results are included, with key parts formally verified in Lean. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show perfect spatial strategy existence in nonlocal games is Σ^0_2-complete, a tight classification with trace costing one existential quantifier, and report Lean formal verification.

entry.title: Forecasting unstructured PDEs on superconducting quantum processors
entry.summary: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper implements a quantum reservoir network (QRN) on IBM superconducting hardware using up to 52 qubits to forecast high-dimensional unstructured partial differential equations. The method is gradient-free and uses partial measure-and-reset so circuit runtime can reach about 24 times the qubit coherence time. On a 2D cylinder flow and a Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion problem, adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduced prediction error by 21% to 43%, and closed-loop autoregressive forecasting was demonstrated. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a gradient-free quantum reservoir network to unstructured PDE forecasting on 52-qubit hardware, reporting 21%-43% error reduction over an autoencoder baseline.

entry.title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination: AI-optimized quantum measurement extracts more information per photon
entry.summary: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination arXiv · Nov 7, 2026The paper proposes a trainable quantum measurement for vision tasks under photon-limited and noisy conditions, consisting of a diffractive optical neural network followed by a detector array. It is trained to maximize the rate at which discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The measurement achieves exponentially lower error than direct imaging and a network optimized for single-photon discrimination, and the advantage is validated in noiseless and electron-multiplying CCD photon-counting experiments. ★★★★ Notable: The authors train a diffractive optical network with a quantum objective, reporting exponentially lower error than imaging and validation in an EMCCD photon-counting experiment.

entry.title: Arrival-time problem in quantum information: observing a Zeno crossover in monitored distributions
entry.summary: Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions arXiv · Nov 7, 2026This paper studies when quantum particles arrive at a detector in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. It identifies a quantum Zeno regime and a low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. The authors measured arrival-time distributions on superconducting quantum hardware in one- and two-dimensional circuits, finding close agreement with quantum-trajectory theory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors study arrival times in periodically monitored spin chains, report Zeno and low-monitoring regimes, and measure distributions on superconducting hardware matching quantum-trajectory theory.

entry.title: Open quantum time crystals that need no external thermodynamic resources, with go and no-go theorems
entry.summary: Open Quantum Time Crystals without External Thermodynamic Resources: Go and No-Go Theorems arXiv · Nov 6, 2026This paper asks whether coupling a quantum system to an environment, without supplying external work or energetic coherence, can produce a time crystal that the isolated system lacks. The authors construct an explicit model and prove that such activation is possible under time-independent Hamiltonian and jump operators, time-translation covariance, and detailed balance, and give several implementations. They also prove a no-go theorem showing that under these conditions activation can only arise from an environment-induced Hamiltonian term, not from dissipation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that environment coupling can activate a time crystal under Lindblad dynamics with no external resources, and give a corresponding no-go theorem.

entry.title: Adaptive Quantization for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
entry.summary: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies policy evaluation with linear function approximation when an agent sends quantized temporal-difference learning updates to a server over a finite-capacity channel. The authors propose BAQ-TD, which combines batching to reduce transmitted variance with adaptive quantization to encode innovations. They prove a high-probability finite-time error bound showing that, above a certain channel capacity, BAQ-TD matches unquantized TD's convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. The method needs O(d log T) bits over horizon T to reach the order-optimal rate. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose BAQ-TD, using batching and adaptive quantization over a finite-capacity channel, with a high-probability finite-time bound and an exponential communication-complexity improvement.

entry.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable? A paper on how fine-tuning a language model in one domain shifts its behavior in others.
entry.summary: Is Persona Generalization Predictable? arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper studies persona generalization, where fine-tuning a language model in one domain changes its behavior in other domains, such as the broadly unsafe behavior seen in emergent misalignment. The authors find that in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates follow an approximately probit-linear relationship across fine-tuning hyperparameters, and that this relationship is roughly shared across model families and sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Changing which layers are fine-tuned alters the slope; for unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields a shallower slope. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a probit-linear in-domain/out-of-domain relation across hyperparameters and model families, unifying emergent misalignment analyses.

entry.title: A short proof of a conjecture on quantum query complexity and deterministic algorithms
entry.summary: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper gives a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which relates the quantum query complexity of partial Boolean functions to the number of queries deterministic algorithms need. The proof uses the completion framework and yields a more general bound based on the classical adversary measure. The authors also derive a stronger variant, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, in an appendix. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture via completion, bounding in terms of classical adversary measure and deriving the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture.

entry.title: Paper showing learning rate decay can exponentially speed up SGD for global nonconvex optimization
entry.summary: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper examines whether learning rate decay in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) gives an asymptotic advantage for global optimization of nonconvex functions. The authors identify a natural class of nonconvex functions, including many popular benchmarks, where SGD with decay needs exponentially fewer gradient queries than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step regime. They also show that annealing solves the associated non-log-concave sampling problem in polynomial time, using weak Poincaré inequalities. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove exponential speedup for SGD with learning rate decay on nonconvex global optimization, analyzed via weak Poincaré inequalities.

entry.title: Succinct Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Shown BQP-Complete
entry.summary: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper studies two basic computational problems in linear systems: evaluating infinite-horizon output energy for autonomous systems, characterized by Lyapunov equations, and computing optimal value functions for controlled systems, characterized by algebraic Riccati equations. System matrices are sparse and encoded succinctly by Boolean circuits, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. The authors prove the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV) is BQP-hard and give a quantum algorithm for the more general succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV), so both are BQP-complete. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that succinct infinite-horizon Lyapunov and LQR value problems are BQP-complete, with a quantum algorithm and a hardness reduction.

entry.title: Showing that EQP ⊆ IP does not relativize
entry.summary: mathsfEQPsubseteqmathsfIP Does Not Relativize arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper builds a recursive oracle O and a unary language L that lies in EQP^O but outside both IP^O and PH^O. This strengthens the BQP versus IP oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. The separation uses a variant of Forrelation in which the normalized correlation is promised to be exactly +1/2 or -1/2. A uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm distinguishes the two cases with certainty using only three oracle queries. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the BQP versus IP oracle separation to exact quantum computation, using an Forrelation variant with exact correlations and a repair method; a three-query algorithm is reported.

entry.title: Computing fair item allocations within budget limits in polynomial time
entry.summary: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies dividing indivisible items fairly among agents with budget constraints and additive valuations, requiring envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) between agents and toward a charity holding unallocated items. The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for computing EF1 allocations under heterogeneous valuations. They also prove that detecting an EF1 violation is NP-complete and provide polynomial-time algorithms for EFX in two special valuation settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open problem by giving a polynomial-time EF1 algorithm under budget constraints, plus NP-completeness and approximation results.

entry.title: Quantum robustness of expectations under sandwiched Rényi divergence limits
entry.summary: Quantum Robustness via Sandwiched Rényi Divergences arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper asks how much the expectation of an observable can change when a quantum state is known only approximately. It takes the worst-case expectation over all states within a sandwiched Rényi divergence budget of a reference state, for every order in [1/2, ∞]. Convex duality reduces this to a one-dimensional optimization, and a classicalization theorem shows the quantum problem matches a classical one under a suitable probability measure. Classical Hoeffding, Bernstein and Markov–Krein bounds therefore carry over. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce worst-case quantum expectations under sandwiched Rényi divergence to a classical problem, transferring classical concentration bounds and showing variance deflation from noncommutat

entry.title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Local-Decoder DQI
entry.summary: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) on random D-regular k-sparse instances, which reduces optimization and Gibbs-measure sampling to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. Using statistical-physics phase transitions, the authors show that local decoders cannot recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold, while belief propagation with quantum messages reaches that threshold. They also show the optimal decoder succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold, suggesting local-decoder DQI gives no exponential speedup for these tasks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link DQI decoding thresholds to tree reconstruction and condensation transitions, proving a local-decoder information obstruction and a tight bound for the optimal decoder.

entry.title: Hidden Tails: Verifying Tail-Risk Claims When Some Outcomes Are Unobserved
entry.summary: Hidden Tails: Certifying Tail-Risk Claims under Selective Labels arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper addresses how past decisions hide some outcomes, which can conceal a predictor's largest errors and leave population tail risk unresolved. The authors derive sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk for binary outcomes and bounded losses, under a stated limit on how outcome odds differ between observed and hidden cases. In controlled experiments with known loan repayments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removed a median 61% of estimated ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive sharp conditional value-at-risk bounds under selective labels and a minimum-cost audit allocation, tested in controlled loan-repayment masking experiments.

entry.title: GeoScope: a training-free method for counting and spatial questions on ultra-high-resolution satellite images
entry.summary: GeoScope: Training-Free Program Execution beyond the Counting Horizon for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Question Answering arXiv · Nov 10, 2026The paper finds that vision-language models undercount objects in ultra-high-resolution remote sensing images once a view contains more than about five objects, and that this limit narrows as views grow. GeoScope has a text-only language model turn each question into a spatial program that sets the region and resolution, while the vision-language model only grounds and counts within its effective range and directions are computed from the grounded boxes. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 points on spatial relations on XLRS-Bench. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a training-free method splitting views by a measured VLM counting limit, reporting large gains on several UHR remote sensing benchmarks.

entry.title: Generalized adaptive boosting and the geometry of mistakes
entry.summary: Generalized Adaptive Boosting and the Geometry of Mistakes arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper extends classical boosting to treat false positives and false negatives separately, introducing a "Z-learner" that guarantees a joint pair of error rates lying in a set Z. It gives a complete geometric characterization of which sets Z can be boosted, unifying the classical result with a recent multi-objective extension. The authors also present an adaptive algorithm that works without knowing Z in advance, and show that Z-learners can amplify confidence, using the centerpoint theorem from computational geometry. ★★★★ Notable: The authors generalize weak learning to joint FP/FN guarantees over a set Z, giving a complete geometric characterization of boostable sets that unifies prior results.

entry.title: Average vs. expected causal effects when individuals influence each other: modeling choices and estimation limits
entry.summary: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper studies causal inference when one person's treatment can affect others' outcomes, a situation called interference. The authors organize their assumptions into three layers (interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models) and split potential outcomes into direct, spillover, and interaction components. They distinguish average causal effects, which compare outcomes under fixed conditions, from expected causal effects, which compare outcomes under a specified allocation policy, and bound the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator for both. They also propose graph-aware independent-set designs whose variance bounds are polynomial in the maximum degree. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose hierarchical finite-population models separating ACEs and ECEs, and report variance bounds contrasting exponential and polynomial sample-size growth under interference.

entry.title: Interpretability Tools Are Not Model-Specific: Transferring Refusal and Read-out Directions Across Models
entry.summary: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper tests whether interpretability tools can move between language models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. It transfers a refusal direction and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 model pairs from five families spanning 1B to 72B parameters. The amount transferred depends on the data the map was fit on, and adding unlabeled prompts from the tool's operating region substantially raises recovery. ★★★★ Notable: The authors transfer interpretability tools via residual-stream maps fit on unlabeled prompts, validated across 110 model pairs with controls and a proof plus coverage score.

entry.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Tiling and Resolution for Small Object Detection
entry.summary: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection arXiv · Nov 10, 2026This paper examines when sliced inference, such as SAHI, actually improves small object detection in high-resolution images.
